Developed by Caroline Wang and Mary Ann Burris in health promotion research, it aims to record community strengths and problems, foster critical dialogue, and reach policymakers with participants' own images and captions. It is as much an empowerment and advocacy method as a data collection technique.

title: Why use images alongside written field notes?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why use images alongside written field notes?
Answer: Photographs and video capture spatial layout, appearance, artifacts, and simultaneous action with a completeness and precision that prose cannot, and they preserve details the observer did not consciously notice at the time. Images also aid memory when writing up, support elicitation in later interviews, and let readers see aspects of the setting directly. Notes remain essential, however, because images do not record meaning, sequence of understanding, or the researcher's situated interpretations.

title: Can drawings, sketches, and maps serve as ethnographic data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Can drawings, sketches, and maps serve as ethnographic data?
Answer: Yes; researcher-made sketches of settings, seating arrangements, and movement paths are classic components of field notes, and participant-drawn maps or timelines reveal how people mentally organize their worlds. Drawing can be used where cameras are intrusive or prohibited, and the act of drawing slows observation in ways many ethnographers find analytically productive. Like photographs, such materials are interpreted in context rather than treated as objective records.

title: What is participatory video in research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is participatory video in research?
Answer: Participatory video hands video production to participants, who plan, shoot, and often edit films about their own lives and issues, with the researcher acting as facilitator. The process reveals what participants consider worth showing and how they choose to represent themselves, which is itself data, and the resulting films can carry their perspectives to wider audiences. It is used in development, community, and youth research where shifting representational control to participants is a methodological and ethical goal.

title: How does photo elicitation change the dynamics of an interview?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does photo elicitation change the dynamics of an interview?
Answer: Anchoring talk in concrete images grounds the interview in specifics rather than generalities, evokes sensory and emotional memory, and gives participants an expert role as interpreters of their own pictures, flattening the usual interviewer-led hierarchy. Research on the technique, going back to John Collier's early work, suggests photo interviews run longer, range wider, and surface different content than question-only interviews. The images function as a third party in the room, easing discussion of difficult topics because attention rests on the picture rather than face-to-face interrogation.

title: What ethical issues arise when photographing or filming identifiable people?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What ethical issues arise when photographing or filming identifiable people?
Answer: Images defeat ordinary anonymization: a face identifies a person permanently, so consent must cover not only being recorded but how images will be stored, shown, and published, and for how long. Special care applies to children, people who cannot consent, bystanders who wander into frame, and settings where being seen there is itself compromising. Common safeguards include consent forms with tiered permissions for different uses, blurring or cropping for publication, participant review of images before use, and agreements on deletion.

title: How is video data from field settings typically analyzed?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How is video data from field settings typically analyzed?
Answer: Analysts first log and index the corpus, creating content summaries with timestamps, then select episodes relevant to the research question for intensive analysis. Selected fragments are viewed repeatedly, often frame by frame, and transcribed in detail, capturing talk alongside gaze, gesture, body position, and object handling, in traditions such as interaction analysis and conversation analysis. Data sessions, where a group of researchers views fragments together, are a common practice for disciplining interpretation and generating alternative readings.

title: How can ethnographers systematically attend to smell, sound, taste, and touch in fieldwork?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can ethnographers systematically attend to smell, sound, taste, and touch in fieldwork?
Answer: Practically, they include sensory registers as explicit categories in observation guides and field notes, describing soundscapes, odors, textures, temperatures, and bodily sensations of activities rather than defaulting to visual description. They apprentice themselves to sensory practices, learning to taste, listen, or handle materials as members do, and use elicitation techniques such as walking with participants or discussing foods, recordings, and objects. Audio recording, and notes on their own bodily responses, extend the record beyond what language easily captures.

title: What is soundscape research in ethnographic work?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is soundscape research in ethnographic work?
Answer: Soundscape research studies the acoustic environment of a place, its voices, machines, signals, music, and silences, and how people produce, perceive, and are governed by it; the term was popularized by R. Murray Schafer. Ethnographers document soundscapes through field recording and listening-focused field notes, and explore members' auditory competencies, such as clinicians monitoring alarm sounds. Sound is analytically valuable because it structures attention, marks territory and time, and carries social meaning that visual observation misses.

title: What is the difference between researcher-generated and participant-generated images?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between researcher-generated and participant-generated images?
Answer: Researcher-generated images reflect the analyst's framing: what the fieldworker judged significant enough to record, useful for systematic documentation of settings and events. Participant-generated images reveal participants' own priorities and self-representations, showing how they see their worlds and what they wish to display or conceal, which is why methods like photovoice rely on them. The two are complementary, and comparing them, what the researcher photographed versus what members photographed, can itself expose divergent perspectives.

title: What is the go-along or walking interview method?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the go-along or walking interview method?
Answer: In a go-along, the researcher accompanies a participant on a natural journey through their environment, a commute, errands, a neighborhood walk, observing and conversing as places prompt commentary. The moving environment acts as a continuous elicitation device, surfacing place-based memories, routines, and sensory experiences that seated interviews rarely reach. Introduced influentially by Margarethe Kusenbach, go-alongs are widely used in urban, health, and sensory ethnography to study how people relate to place.

title: How does Sarah Pink characterize sensory ethnography?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does Sarah Pink characterize sensory ethnography?
Answer: Sarah Pink presents sensory ethnography not as a separate technique but as a re-thinking of ethnography itself, in which perception is understood as multisensory and emplaced, and the researcher's own body becomes a research instrument through shared activities with participants. She emphasizes learning through participation, doing, moving, and sensing along with people, over detached observation, and encourages media such as video and audio that can evoke sensory experience for audiences. Her framework draws on phenomenological anthropology, including the work of scholars like Tim Ingold and David Howes's culture-of-the-senses tradition.

title: What epistemological problems arise in treating photographs as evidence?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What epistemological problems arise in treating photographs as evidence?
Answer: A photograph is indexically linked to what stood before the lens, yet it is thoroughly constructed: framing, timing, angle, and selection determine what appears, and meaning is supplied by captions and viewing contexts rather than residing in the image. Treating photos as transparent windows therefore smuggles in the photographer's choices as if they were the world's own features. Visual methodologists respond by analyzing images as situated productions, documenting how, why, and by whom each image was made, and triangulating visual materials with observation and talk rather than letting pictures stand as self-sufficient proof.

title: How does multimodal transcription capture embodied conduct in video analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How does multimodal transcription capture embodied conduct in video analysis?
Answer: Multimodal transcription extends conventional talk transcripts with aligned notation of gaze direction, gesture, body orientation, movement, and object manipulation, often using timeline layouts, frame grabs, or annotation conventions developed in interaction research such as those of Lorenza Mondada. The point is analytic: much coordination in interaction is achieved bodily and materially, so a words-only transcript misrepresents how the event worked. Transcription choices are themselves theoretical commitments about what matters, so analysts specify their conventions and accept that any transcript is a selective rendering of the recording.

title: What consent issues surround the reuse and publication of visual data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What consent issues surround the reuse and publication of visual data?
Answer: Consent given for recording does not automatically extend to conference display, publication, teaching use, online circulation, or archiving, each of which exposes identifiable participants differently and, once online, irreversibly. Best practice uses tiered consent specifying permitted uses, revisits consent before new uses, and offers options such as blurring, stills instead of moving images, or exclusion from publication while remaining in analysis. Researchers must also consider third parties in frame, platform terms for found images, and the impossibility of genuinely withdrawing an image after digital release, which argues for conservative publication choices with sensitive material.

title: How can sensory ethnographic findings be made systematic rather than merely evocative?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Visual & sensory ethnography
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How can sensory ethnographic findings be made systematic rather than merely evocative?
Answer: Systematization comes from treating sensory data with the same discipline as any other: recording sensory observations consistently across occasions using structured registers, linking the researcher's sensations to members' own sensory categories and vocabularies elicited in the field, and comparing sensory patterns across times, places, and participants. Claims should rest on demonstrated sensory orders in the setting, such as how workers actually use smell to make decisions, evidenced through observation, apprenticeship, and elicitation, rather than on the researcher's impressions alone. Transparent method sections describing how sensory data were generated and analyzed allow readers to assess the claims, moving sensory work from atmosphere to evidence.

title: What does "leaving the field" mean in ethnographic research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does "leaving the field" mean in ethnographic research?
Answer: Leaving the field is the phase in which the researcher ends regular presence in the setting and disengages from fieldwork relationships. It involves practical steps, such as final data collection and farewells, and relational ones, including explaining the departure and honoring commitments made during the study. Methodologists treat exit as a stage requiring as much care as entry, because it affects participants, the data, and the setting's openness to future researchers.

title: Why should researchers plan their exit from the field in advance?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why should researchers plan their exit from the field in advance?
Answer: An abrupt or unexplained departure can leave participants feeling used or abandoned, especially after months of built relationships, and it can foreclose returning to check interpretations or collect missing data. Planning allows the researcher to signal the ending gradually, complete promised obligations such as reports or help, and close relationships respectfully. It also protects the setting's goodwill toward research generally, which later investigators may depend on.

title: What is informed consent in fieldwork?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is informed consent in fieldwork?
Answer: Informed consent means that participants understand who the researcher is, what the study is about, what participation involves, and any risks, and that they agree voluntarily, knowing they can withdraw. In ethnography, consent is usually obtained through explanation and agreement at entry and then maintained conversationally over time, since fieldwork evolves and new people appear. Written forms may be used, but in many field settings verbal, documented consent is more appropriate and equally valid ethically.

title: What does anonymization involve in ethnographic reporting?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does anonymization involve in ethnographic reporting?
Answer: Anonymization removes or disguises information that could identify participants and, often, the setting itself: names are replaced with pseudonyms, and details such as locations, job titles, dates, and distinctive events are altered or generalized. The aim is to let readers understand the findings without enabling them to identify the people described. Ethnographers must balance disguise against accuracy, changing only details that do not affect the analysis, and they disclose that such disguising was done.

title: Why are pseudonyms used for people and places in ethnographies?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why are pseudonyms used for people and places in ethnographies?
Answer: Pseudonyms protect participants from the consequences of being identifiable in published accounts, which may describe private behavior, conflicts, rule-breaking, or unflattering events. They also protect settings, since organizations and communities can suffer reputational harm from research portraits. Classic community studies established the convention of pseudonymous towns and members, and it remains standard unless participants explicitly choose to be named.

title: What is member checking after fieldwork?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is member checking after fieldwork?
Answer: Member checking means returning findings, interpretations, or draft text to participants so they can confirm, correct, or contest how they and their world are represented. It serves validity, catching factual errors and misreadings, and ethics, giving people a voice in accounts about them. Researchers must decide in advance how disagreements will be handled, since participants may dispute interpretations the researcher believes are well founded, and outright veto power is generally not promised.

title: Should researchers stay in contact with participants after fieldwork ends?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Should researchers stay in contact with participants after fieldwork ends?
Answer: There is no single rule: some relationships naturally continue as friendships or professional ties, and many ethnographers maintain contact, return findings, or revisit the field for follow-up studies. What matters ethically is honesty about the changed relationship, not creating expectations of continued involvement that will not be met, and continuing to protect confidences after leaving. Researchers should decide their approach deliberately and communicate it, rather than drifting into silence after intense engagement.

title: What does the principle of doing no harm require in ethnography?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does the principle of doing no harm require in ethnography?
Answer: The principle requires researchers to anticipate and minimize the risks their presence, questions, and publications create for participants, including social, psychological, legal, economic, and reputational harms. In fieldwork this means care about what is asked and witnessed, protection of confidences within the setting, and secure data handling; in writing it means considering how depictions could hurt the people and communities described. Because harms can arise long after fieldwork, the obligation extends through publication and beyond.

title: How can a researcher disengage from the field gradually rather than abruptly?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can a researcher disengage from the field gradually rather than abruptly?
Answer: Gradual disengagement involves announcing the ending well in advance, reducing visit frequency over weeks rather than disappearing, completing promised tasks and reciprocities, and creating closure rituals such as farewell gatherings or thank-you visits. Researchers often shift their role in the final phase toward checking interpretations and filling data gaps, which naturally signals the study's completion. Documenting the exit in field notes is also advised, since departures reveal how the researcher had come to be positioned in the setting.

title: What obligations do researchers have to share findings with the communities they studied?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What obligations do researchers have to share findings with the communities they studied?
Answer: Many ethics codes and most methodologists recognize an obligation of return: participants gave time and access, and deserve access to what was learned, in a form they can use, such as plain-language summaries, presentations, or community meetings, not just academic articles. Feedback also allows correction of errors and demonstrates respect, though researchers must prepare for findings to be unwelcome to some. The commitment, including its form and timing, is best negotiated at access and honored at exit.

title: What emotional dimensions accompany leaving the field?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What emotional dimensions accompany leaving the field?
Answer: Long fieldwork creates genuine attachments, so departure commonly brings grief, guilt, and role confusion for researchers, and feelings of loss or abandonment among participants who came to value the relationship. Researchers may also feel relief entangled with guilt, particularly when leaving difficult settings for comfortable academic life while participants remain. Acknowledging these emotions, in supervision, peer debriefing, and the field diary, is considered part of competent practice, both for the researcher's wellbeing and because emotional responses carry analytic information about the field relationships.

title: How does covert research complicate fieldwork ethics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does covert research complicate fieldwork ethics?
Answer: Covert research denies participants informed consent, involves sustained deception of people who may have extended trust and friendship, and makes ethical exit nearly impossible, since leaving either perpetuates the lie or inflicts the injury of revelation. It also endangers the researcher and future research access if exposed. Ethics codes therefore restrict covert methods to cases where the knowledge is significant, obtainable no other way, and low-risk to participants, and require justification before an ethics committee rather than the researcher's own judgment alone.

title: What is process consent and why does it suit ethnographic research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is process consent and why does it suit ethnographic research?
Answer: Process consent treats consent as an ongoing negotiation rather than a one-time signature: the researcher revisits agreement as the study evolves, before observing new kinds of situations, when new people enter the setting, and at sensitive moments. It suits ethnography because fieldwork's open-ended, emergent character means participants cannot meaningfully consent at entry to everything that will later occur. Practically it involves periodic reminders of the research role, renewed permission at key junctures, and respect for momentary refusals without penalty.

title: How should researchers handle guilty knowledge acquired in the field?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should researchers handle guilty knowledge acquired in the field?
Answer: Guilty knowledge, awareness of participants' rule-breaking, secrets, or discreditable acts, is almost inevitable in close fieldwork, and handling it requires forethought: researchers decide before entry what they can keep confidential, state any limits, such as serious harm to others or legally mandated reporting, and otherwise protect confidences rigorously, including from other participants and from gatekeepers. In publications, such material is used only when analytically necessary and heavily protected against identification. Carrying guilty knowledge is also an emotional burden, best managed through supervision and clear personal boundaries.

title: How can anonymization fail even when names are changed?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can anonymization fail even when names are changed?
Answer: Deductive disclosure occurs when combinations of unaltered details, a role, a distinctive event, a place description, allow insiders or motivated outsiders to identify people or sites despite pseudonyms; in small or unique settings, the organization itself is often recognizable, which then narrows individual identities. Members of a studied community can almost always identify each other in the text, so internal confidentiality is frequently the harder problem than protection from strangers. Mitigations include altering non-essential details, aggregating or omitting rare characteristics, checking drafts against an insider's eye, and being honest with participants about the realistic limits of disguise.

title: What role do ethics committees play in approving ethnographic research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What role do ethics committees play in approving ethnographic research?
Answer: Ethics committees review fieldwork plans for consent procedures, risk to participants, data protection, and researcher safety before the study begins, and researchers must report significant changes as the emergent design evolves. The review model, built around fixed protocols and signed forms, fits ethnography imperfectly, since fieldworkers cannot specify in advance whom they will meet or what will happen, so applications typically describe procedures and principles, such as process consent, rather than exact instruments. Approval is a floor, not the ceiling: situated ethical judgment in the field remains the researcher's continuing responsibility.

title: How should an ethnographer manage the dilemma of witnessing serious wrongdoing while bound by confidentiality?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How should an ethnographer manage the dilemma of witnessing serious wrongdoing while bound by confidentiality?
Answer: The dilemma pits promised confidentiality, the foundation of field trust, against duties to prevent harm and, sometimes, legal obligations to report or testify; there is no formula, but accepted practice is anticipatory: define before entry which acts fall outside confidentiality, communicate those limits during consent, and know the jurisdiction's mandatory reporting and subpoena exposure, since field notes are not legally privileged in most systems. When the situation arises, the researcher weighs the immediacy and severity of harm, options short of formal reporting such as direct intervention or persuading actors to stop, and the consequences for everyone protected by the study's confidentiality. Whatever is decided must be documentable as a reasoned ethical judgment, ideally taken with advice from supervisors or the ethics committee.

title: What ethical questions surround friendship and intimacy in long-term field relationships?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What ethical questions surround friendship and intimacy in long-term field relationships?
Answer: Long fieldwork blurs the line between rapport and friendship, raising questions about whether closeness is authentic or instrumental, whether intimate disclosures made to a friend may be used as data from a researcher, and what is owed when the study ends and the researcher's attention moves on. Critics have called cultivated rapport a form of manipulation, faking friendship for data, while others defend genuine dual relationships if handled transparently. Widely endorsed safeguards include reminding intimates of the research role before sensitive material becomes data, excluding confidences shared clearly in friendship, and refusing to let the exit erase obligations the relationship created.

title: How can ethnographers reconcile participant protection with data archiving and open science expectations?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How can ethnographers reconcile participant protection with data archiving and open science expectations?
Answer: Funders and journals increasingly expect data sharing, but ethnographic materials, field notes, recordings, detailed contexts, resist anonymization, since removing identifying texture often destroys the data's meaning, and participants rarely consented to open deposit. Practical reconciliations include tiered access archives with vetted-user controls and embargoes, sharing only selected, prepared materials rather than raw notes, building explicit archiving options into consent from the start, and publishing rich methodological documentation instead of raw data where risks are unmanageable. Most guidelines now accept that legitimate ethical constraints can justify not sharing, provided the decision is explained rather than assumed.

title: What are a researcher's obligations when findings could harm the community they studied?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Ethnography & Observation
Subcategory: Leaving the field & fieldwork ethics
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What are a researcher's obligations when findings could harm the community they studied?
Answer: Publication can expose a community to stigma, policing, policy backlash, or internal conflict, so researchers must weigh scholarly and public value against foreseeable collective harms, a calculus individual-focused ethics review handles poorly. Recognized practices include consulting community members about sensitive findings before publication, contextualizing negative findings carefully to prevent misuse, strengthening disguise of the community's identity, timing or venue choices that reduce sensational uptake, and in extreme cases withholding specific material. The researcher remains responsible for reasonably foreseeable uses of their work, and honest engagement with the community about the trade-offs is generally considered preferable to either silent publication or silent suppression.

title: What is a diary study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a diary study?
Answer: A diary study is a data collection method in which participants record their experiences, activities, thoughts, or feelings over a period of time, usually at regular intervals or when relevant events occur. Because entries are made close in time to the experiences they describe, diaries reduce the memory distortions that affect retrospective interviews. Diary studies are especially useful for capturing everyday routines, fluctuating states, and private behaviors that researchers cannot easily observe directly.

title: What is the experience sampling method?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the experience sampling method?
Answer: The experience sampling method (ESM) asks participants to report on their current thoughts, feelings, or activities at multiple moments throughout daily life, often when prompted by a signal such as a smartphone notification. By sampling experiences in the moment and in natural settings, ESM captures how states vary across time and context rather than relying on a single summary judgment. It is widely used to study mood, well-being, work experiences, and social interactions.

title: What is the difference between a solicited and an unsolicited diary?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between a solicited and an unsolicited diary?
Answer: A solicited diary is created at the researcher's request specifically for a study, with participants given instructions about what and when to record. An unsolicited diary is a pre-existing personal document, such as a private journal, that was written for the diarist's own purposes and is later analyzed as data. Solicited diaries give researchers control over structure and timing, while unsolicited diaries offer naturally occurring accounts untouched by the research process.

title: What is ecological momentary assessment?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is ecological momentary assessment?
Answer: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) is a family of methods, closely related to experience sampling, in which participants repeatedly report on symptoms, behaviors, or experiences in real time within their natural environments. The term is used mainly in health and psychology research, and reports are often collected via mobile devices. EMA aims to maximize ecological validity and minimize recall bias by capturing phenomena as they happen in everyday life.

title: What are the main advantages of diary methods over one-off interviews?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What are the main advantages of diary methods over one-off interviews?
Answer: Diary methods capture experiences close to when they occur, which reduces recall bias and memory decay compared with retrospective interviews. They document change and variability over time, revealing patterns and fluctuations that a single interview would miss. Diaries can also access private, mundane, or sensitive aspects of daily life that participants might forget or consider too trivial to mention in a formal interview.

title: What formats can research diaries take?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What formats can research diaries take?
Answer: Research diaries can be kept in many formats, including paper booklets, online forms, smartphone apps, text messages, audio recordings, video entries, and photo diaries. The choice depends on participants' preferences and skills, the type of experience being studied, and practical issues such as cost and data security. Audio and photo formats can lower the burden for participants who find writing difficult and can capture richer contextual detail.

title: How long does a typical diary study last?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How long does a typical diary study last?
Answer: Diary studies commonly run from a few days to several weeks, with one to two weeks being a frequent choice because it balances data richness against participant fatigue. The appropriate duration depends on how often the phenomenon of interest occurs; rare events require longer windows, while frequent daily experiences can be captured in shorter periods. Researchers must weigh the value of longer observation against declining compliance and entry quality over time.

title: What kinds of research questions are diary studies best suited to answer?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What kinds of research questions are diary studies best suited to answer?
Answer: Diary studies suit questions about processes, routines, and experiences that unfold over time, such as how people manage chronic illness day to day, how mood varies with daily events, or how technology is used in everyday contexts. They are also valuable when behavior is private, dispersed across settings, or hard for an observer to access. Questions requiring a single retrospective summary or deep interactive probing are usually better served by interviews.

title: What is the difference between signal-contingent, event-contingent, and interval-contingent sampling in diary research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between signal-contingent, event-contingent, and interval-contingent sampling in diary research?
Answer: In signal-contingent sampling, participants complete a report whenever they receive a prompt, often delivered at random times to sample a representative slice of experience. In event-contingent sampling, participants make an entry each time a predefined event occurs, such as a social interaction or a craving. In interval-contingent sampling, entries are completed at fixed, predictable times, such as every evening. The choice depends on whether the researcher wants representative moments, complete coverage of specific events, or regular summaries.

title: How can researchers reduce participant burden in diary and experience sampling studies?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can researchers reduce participant burden in diary and experience sampling studies?
Answer: Burden can be reduced by keeping each entry short and focused, limiting the number of daily prompts, choosing convenient recording formats such as mobile apps or voice memos, and restricting the study to the shortest duration that answers the question. Clear instructions, practice entries, and flexible timing windows also help. Because high burden leads to missed entries and superficial responses, minimizing it protects both data quality and participant retention.

title: What is the diary-interview method?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the diary-interview method?
Answer: The diary-interview method combines a period of diary keeping with a follow-up interview in which the researcher and participant discuss the diary entries together. The diary provides a detailed record of events and experiences, and the interview allows the researcher to probe meanings, fill gaps, and explore entries in depth. This combination pairs the temporal precision of diaries with the interpretive richness of interviews.

title: What compliance problems arise in diary studies and how are they detected?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What compliance problems arise in diary studies and how are they detected?
Answer: Common compliance problems include missed entries, retrospective backfilling in which participants complete several entries at once from memory, and increasingly brief or careless responses over time. Electronic diaries help detect these problems because they timestamp each entry, revealing when reports were actually completed. Researchers can also monitor response rates during the study and contact participants early if compliance drops.

title: How do diary methods reduce retrospective recall bias?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How do diary methods reduce retrospective recall bias?
Answer: Retrospective recall bias occurs when people reconstruct past experiences inaccurately, often influenced by their current mood, salient peak moments, or general beliefs about themselves. Diary methods shorten the interval between experience and report, sometimes to minutes, so accounts rely less on reconstruction and more on immediate awareness. This makes diaries particularly valuable for studying transient states like pain, emotion, or momentary decisions that are poorly remembered later.

title: What should researchers consider when designing diary entry prompts?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What should researchers consider when designing diary entry prompts?
Answer: Prompts should be clear, specific, and quick to answer, using language participants understand and focusing on the experiences central to the research question. Researchers must decide how structured entries will be, ranging from open free-text reflections to fixed questions, balancing richness against comparability and burden. Piloting the prompts with a few participants helps reveal ambiguous wording, excessive length, and mismatches with how people actually experience their days.

title: How can researchers keep participants engaged across a multi-week diary study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can researchers keep participants engaged across a multi-week diary study?
Answer: Engagement strategies include regular friendly reminders, brief check-ins or mid-study contact from the researcher, staged incentives that reward sustained participation, and showing participants that their entries are valued. Making the diary easy and even enjoyable to complete, for example through a well-designed app or the option to use voice or photos, also sustains motivation. Anticipating fatigue in the design stage is more effective than trying to rescue a study after compliance collapses.

title: What are audio diaries and when are they preferable to written diaries?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are audio diaries and when are they preferable to written diaries?
Answer: Audio diaries are spoken entries that participants record, typically on a phone or voice recorder, instead of writing. They are preferable when participants have limited literacy, limited time, or conditions that make writing difficult, and when the researcher values spontaneous, expressive accounts with tone of voice and emotion. Audio entries are often longer and more narrative than written ones, though they require transcription and may raise privacy concerns if recorded in shared spaces.

title: What is measurement reactivity in diary research and how can it be assessed?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is measurement reactivity in diary research and how can it be assessed?
Answer: Measurement reactivity occurs when the act of repeatedly recording experiences changes the phenomenon being studied, for example when logging food intake alters eating behavior or reflecting on mood changes emotional patterns. Reactivity can be assessed by examining whether responses systematically drift over the diary period, by comparing groups with different reporting frequencies, or by triangulating with unobtrusive measures. Some reactivity is unavoidable, so researchers should report it as a limitation and consider whether it threatens their specific conclusions.

title: How does experience sampling enable analysis of within-person variability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How does experience sampling enable analysis of within-person variability?
Answer: Because experience sampling collects many repeated observations from each participant, researchers can distinguish differences between people from fluctuations within the same person across time and situations. This allows questions such as whether an individual's stress rises on days with more social conflict, which cross-sectional designs cannot answer. Analytically, such data are typically treated as hierarchically nested, with moments nested within persons, and in qualitative analysis they support case-by-case examination of each participant's temporal patterns.

title: How can qualitative depth be combined with the structured repetition of experience sampling?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How can qualitative depth be combined with the structured repetition of experience sampling?
Answer: Researchers can embed open-ended text or voice prompts within structured momentary surveys, inviting brief narratives about what is happening and why it matters. They can also follow the sampling period with elicitation interviews that use the participant's own momentary reports as prompts for deeper reflection, a form of stimulated recall. This hybrid approach preserves the temporal precision of sampling while recovering the meaning-making that fixed response scales cannot capture.

title: How should researchers handle missing entries and fatigue effects when interpreting diary data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Diary & experience sampling methods
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How should researchers handle missing entries and fatigue effects when interpreting diary data?
Answer: Missing entries in diary studies are rarely random; participants tend to skip reports precisely when they are busiest, most distressed, or least engaged, which can bias the picture of daily life toward calmer moments. Researchers should examine patterns of missingness, compare early and late study periods for signs of fatigue such as shorter entries, and interpret findings in light of these patterns. In qualitative diary analysis, gaps themselves can be treated as meaningful and explored in follow-up interviews rather than simply ignored.

title: What is document analysis in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is document analysis in qualitative research?
Answer: Document analysis is a systematic procedure for reviewing and interpreting documents, whether printed or electronic, in order to elicit meaning, gain understanding, and develop empirical knowledge. It involves finding, selecting, appraising, and synthesizing data contained in documents such as reports, letters, policies, or meeting minutes. Document analysis is often used alongside interviews or observation as part of triangulation, but it can also stand alone as the primary method.

title: What types of documents can serve as qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What types of documents can serve as qualitative data?
Answer: Qualitative researchers analyze a wide range of documents, including official records such as policies, minutes, and annual reports; personal documents such as letters, diaries, and memoirs; media materials such as newspapers and advertisements; and organizational artifacts such as manuals, emails, and websites. Documents may be textual, visual, or a combination of both. What unites them is that they were produced for purposes other than the research, making them naturally occurring data.

title: What is the difference between primary and secondary sources in archival research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between primary and secondary sources in archival research?
Answer: A primary source is a document created at the time of the events or by someone with direct involvement, such as an original letter, a court record, or minutes of a meeting. A secondary source interprets, summarizes, or comments on primary material, such as a later historical account or a review article. Archival researchers generally privilege primary sources for evidence about events, while secondary sources provide context and existing interpretations.

title: Why is document analysis considered an unobtrusive method?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why is document analysis considered an unobtrusive method?
Answer: Document analysis is unobtrusive because the documents already exist and were created without the researcher's involvement, so studying them does not alter the behavior being investigated. Unlike interviews or observation, there is no reactivity, since participants cannot adjust their accounts in response to the researcher's presence. This makes documents especially valuable for studying past events, sensitive topics, or official positions as they were actually recorded.

title: What are archival data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What are archival data?
Answer: Archival data are records that have been preserved over time, typically held in archives, libraries, organizational repositories, or digital collections, and later used for research purposes. They include government records, institutional files, personal papers, photographs, and increasingly born-digital materials. Because archival data were created for administrative, legal, or personal purposes rather than research, they offer authentic traces of past activity but require careful appraisal of their origins and completeness.

title: What is the difference between public records and personal documents?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between public records and personal documents?
Answer: Public records are documents produced by governments, courts, and other institutions for official purposes, such as legislation, census reports, and registries, and they are usually formal and standardized. Personal documents are created by individuals for private purposes, such as letters, diaries, photographs, and family papers, and they express subjective experience and perspective. Both are valuable in qualitative research, but they demand different questions about authorship, audience, and intent.

title: What is grey literature?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is grey literature?
Answer: Grey literature refers to materials produced outside commercial or academic publishing channels, such as government reports, working papers, conference proceedings, theses, NGO publications, and technical documents. It is not peer reviewed in the conventional sense but often contains detailed, timely information unavailable elsewhere. Researchers using grey literature should assess the credibility of the producing organization and the transparency of its methods.

title: How are documents used for triangulation in qualitative studies?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How are documents used for triangulation in qualitative studies?
Answer: In triangulation, documents provide an independent line of evidence that can corroborate, elaborate, or contradict what participants say in interviews or what researchers see in observation. For example, meeting minutes can be compared with staff accounts of a decision, revealing convergence or discrepancies worth exploring. Rather than simply confirming findings, documentary evidence often adds historical depth and official framing that enriches interpretation.

title: What are the four criteria commonly used to appraise documentary sources?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the four criteria commonly used to appraise documentary sources?
Answer: A widely used framework, associated with the sociologist John Scott, appraises documents on four criteria: authenticity, whether the document is genuine and of dependable origin; credibility, whether it is free from error and distortion; representativeness, whether it is typical of documents of its kind or a known exception; and meaning, whether its content is clear and interpretable. Applying these criteria helps researchers avoid treating documents as transparent windows onto reality.

title: How should researchers sample documents for a qualitative study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should researchers sample documents for a qualitative study?
Answer: Document sampling should be guided by the research question and an explicit rationale, for example selecting all policy documents on a topic within a date range, purposively choosing information-rich cases, or sampling across document types and producers to capture different perspectives. Researchers should describe their search and inclusion strategy transparently, including where documents were found and what was excluded. Attention to what is missing from the available record is as important as what is present.

title: What ethical issues arise in document and archival research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What ethical issues arise in document and archival research?
Answer: Although documents may be publicly accessible, they can contain identifying or sensitive information about people who never consented to research use, so researchers must consider privacy, potential harm, and any access conditions set by archives. Personal documents such as letters raise questions about the intentions of authors and third parties mentioned in them. Researchers should follow archive regulations, anonymize where appropriate, and weigh the public interest of the research against risks to those documented.

title: What is the difference between manifest and latent content when analyzing documents?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between manifest and latent content when analyzing documents?
Answer: Manifest content is the surface, directly observable content of a document, such as the words used, topics mentioned, or images shown, which can be described and counted with relative objectivity. Latent content is the underlying meaning, tone, or ideology that must be inferred through interpretation, such as the assumptions a policy makes about its target population. Rigorous document analysis usually attends to both levels, making the interpretive moves explicit.

title: Why should organizational documents be treated as social products rather than neutral records?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Why should organizational documents be treated as social products rather than neutral records?
Answer: Organizational documents are written by particular authors, for particular audiences, within conventions and power relations that shape what is recorded and how. Minutes, reports, and policies often present sanitized or strategic versions of events, constructed to justify decisions or project competence. Treating documents as social products means asking who produced them, for whom, under what circumstances, and with what purpose, rather than reading them as straightforward descriptions of what happened.

title: What are the main limitations of relying solely on documents as data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the main limitations of relying solely on documents as data?
Answer: Documents were created for purposes other than research, so they may lack the detail needed to answer the research question, and important matters may never have been written down. Access can be restricted, records may be incomplete or biased toward official perspectives, and the researcher usually cannot ask the author clarifying questions. These limitations are why document analysis is often combined with interviews or observation, though a well-designed documentary study can still stand on its own.

title: What is provenance and why does it matter in archival research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is provenance and why does it matter in archival research?
Answer: Provenance refers to the origin and custodial history of a document or collection: who created it, how it was kept, and how it came to be in the archive. Provenance matters because it underpins judgments about authenticity and helps researchers understand the context in which records were produced and preserved. Archives typically organize collections by provenance, and knowing this history alerts researchers to possible selection, loss, or reordering of materials over time.

title: How can document analysis be combined productively with interviews?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can document analysis be combined productively with interviews?
Answer: Documents can be used before interviews to build background knowledge and generate informed questions, during interviews as elicitation prompts that participants respond to, and after interviews to check accounts against the written record. Conversely, interviews can illuminate how documents were produced and used in practice, revealing the gap between official texts and lived reality. This iterative movement between talk and text often produces stronger interpretations than either source alone.

title: What does it mean to say that documents are active agents rather than inert containers of information?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What does it mean to say that documents are active agents rather than inert containers of information?
Answer: This perspective holds that documents do things in social settings: they circulate, structure activity, confer authority, and mediate relationships, rather than merely storing content. A referral letter, for instance, moves a patient through a healthcare system and shapes how professionals act, independent of any single reader's interpretation. Analyzing documents as active agents shifts attention from content alone to how documents are produced, exchanged, and consumed within networks of action.

title: How should researchers interpret silences and absences in archives?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How should researchers interpret silences and absences in archives?
Answer: Archives systematically underrepresent groups and activities that lacked the power, literacy, or institutional standing to generate and preserve records, so what is absent can be as analytically significant as what is present. Researchers should ask whose voices are missing, whether records were never created, were destroyed, or were excluded by archival selection practices, and how these silences shape the historical narrative. Reading against the grain, seeking alternative sources, and explicitly theorizing absence are established responses to this problem.

title: What methodological issues arise when working with digitized archives and searchable databases?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What methodological issues arise when working with digitized archives and searchable databases?
Answer: Digitization changes what researchers can find and how they find it: keyword search privileges documents containing anticipated terms, optical character recognition errors silently exclude material, and digitized collections are themselves selections shaped by funding and institutional priorities. Researchers may over-sample what is conveniently online and mistake the digital corpus for the full record. Rigorous practice involves documenting search strategies, understanding the scope and gaps of each database, and where possible checking digital findings against original collections.

title: What role does reflexivity play in archival and documentary interpretation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Document & archival analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What role does reflexivity play in archival and documentary interpretation?
Answer: Because documents do not speak for themselves, the researcher's assumptions, categories, and present-day concerns inevitably shape which records seem significant and how they are read. Reflexivity involves making these influences explicit, considering how the researcher's position and the archive's own organization guide interpretation, and remaining open to readings that challenge initial expectations. It also includes acknowledging the temporal gap between the document's world and the researcher's, guarding against anachronistic interpretation.

title: What is an open-ended survey question?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an open-ended survey question?
Answer: An open-ended survey question asks respondents to answer in their own words rather than choosing from predefined options, for example asking what they found most difficult about a service. Such questions capture perspectives, reasons, and experiences the researcher may not have anticipated. The trade-off is that responses vary widely in length and depth and require qualitative analysis rather than simple tabulation.

title: What is a qualitative survey?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a qualitative survey?
Answer: A qualitative survey is a questionnaire composed mainly or entirely of open-ended questions, designed to collect written accounts of experiences, views, and meanings from a relatively large or dispersed group of people. Unlike interviews, responses are self-administered and typed or written by participants themselves, usually online. The resulting textual data are analyzed with qualitative techniques such as thematic analysis.

title: How do open-ended and closed-ended questions differ?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How do open-ended and closed-ended questions differ?
Answer: Closed-ended questions provide fixed response options such as rating scales or multiple choice, producing standardized data that are easy to compare and quantify. Open-ended questions invite free-form answers, producing textual data that reveal how respondents themselves frame an issue. Closed questions constrain answers to the researcher's categories, whereas open questions let unexpected ideas surface at the cost of greater analytic effort.

title: When should a researcher choose a qualitative survey instead of interviews?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: When should a researcher choose a qualitative survey instead of interviews?
Answer: Qualitative surveys are a good choice when the researcher wants a wide range of perspectives from many or geographically dispersed people, when the topic is sensitive enough that anonymity may encourage franker answers, or when time and resources do not allow individual interviews. They also suit participants who prefer writing at their own pace to real-time conversation. Interviews remain preferable when deep probing, rapport, and follow-up questions are essential.

title: What are the main advantages of qualitative surveys?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What are the main advantages of qualitative surveys?
Answer: Qualitative surveys can reach large, diverse, and dispersed samples cheaply, give participants anonymity that may encourage disclosure on sensitive topics, and let people respond at a time and pace of their choosing. They also remove interviewer effects, since there is no interviewer whose presence or reactions could shape answers. For researchers, the data arrive already in written form, eliminating transcription.

title: What are the main disadvantages of open-ended survey questions?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What are the main disadvantages of open-ended survey questions?
Answer: Responses to open-ended survey questions are often brief, and the researcher cannot probe, clarify, or follow up as in an interview, so depth depends entirely on what respondents choose to write. Some respondents skip open questions altogether, and answer quality varies with literacy, motivation, and time. Analysis is also more labor-intensive than for closed questions, since each answer must be read and coded.

title: What is an online qualitative survey?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an online qualitative survey?
Answer: An online qualitative survey delivers open-ended questions through a web platform, allowing participants to type responses on their own devices whenever convenient. Online delivery makes it easy to reach dispersed or hard-to-access populations, to branch questions based on earlier answers, and to collect data quickly at low cost. Researchers must still attend to accessibility, data protection, and the fact that participation is limited to people with internet access and adequate literacy.

title: Can a survey mix open-ended and closed-ended questions?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Can a survey mix open-ended and closed-ended questions?
Answer: Yes, mixed-format surveys are common: closed questions capture standardized information such as demographics or ratings, while open questions gather explanations, examples, and unanticipated views. A frequent design places an open follow-up after a closed item, asking respondents to explain their rating. Researchers should ensure the open questions are genuinely analyzed qualitatively rather than treated as an afterthought.

title: What makes a well-designed open-ended survey item?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What makes a well-designed open-ended survey item?
Answer: A good open-ended item is specific enough to orient the respondent but broad enough to allow diverse answers, uses plain unambiguous language, and asks about one thing at a time. Signaling the kind and amount of detail wanted, for example by inviting an example or a description of a particular occasion, improves response quality. Items should avoid leading phrasing, jargon, and assumptions about the respondent's circumstances.

title: How does question order affect responses in qualitative surveys?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does question order affect responses in qualitative surveys?
Answer: Earlier questions create a frame that shapes how respondents interpret and answer later ones, so placing a strongly evaluative or emotionally charged question first can color the whole survey. Ordering from general to specific helps respondents ease into the topic before tackling detailed or sensitive items, which are usually placed later once some engagement is established. Researchers should also consider fatigue, since open questions near the end of a long survey tend to receive shorter answers.

title: How can researchers encourage richer responses to open-ended survey questions?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can researchers encourage richer responses to open-ended survey questions?
Answer: Response richness improves when the survey explains why detailed answers matter, keeps the total number of open questions modest, and provides generous text boxes that signal longer answers are welcome. Asking about concrete experiences, such as describing a specific recent occasion, elicits more detail than abstract opinion questions. Some researchers also use gentle written prompts within the question, such as inviting examples or reasons, to mimic interview probing.

title: How are open-ended survey responses typically analyzed?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How are open-ended survey responses typically analyzed?
Answer: Open-ended responses are usually analyzed with qualitative techniques such as thematic analysis or qualitative content analysis: researchers read the full dataset, code segments of text, and develop categories or themes that capture patterns of meaning across respondents. Because individual answers are often short, patterns emerge across the breadth of the dataset rather than within any single response. Some studies also report simple counts of how frequently ideas appear, provided the interpretive analysis remains primary.

title: What is a leading question and why should surveys avoid them?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is a leading question and why should surveys avoid them?
Answer: A leading question is worded in a way that suggests a particular answer or embeds an assumption, for example asking what problems a respondent experienced when they may have experienced none. Leading questions bias responses toward the implied position and undermine the credibility of findings. Neutral wording, balanced framing, and pilot testing help detect and remove leading formulations before data collection.

title: Why is piloting important for qualitative questionnaires?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Why is piloting important for qualitative questionnaires?
Answer: Piloting reveals whether questions are understood as intended, whether they elicit the kind and depth of response needed, and how long completion takes. Because there is no interviewer to clarify misunderstandings during self-administration, ambiguities that would be trivial in an interview can ruin survey data. A small pilot with members of the target population, ideally followed by brief feedback about the experience, allows wording, order, and length to be refined before launch.

title: What is satisficing in survey responding and how does it affect open-ended data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is satisficing in survey responding and how does it affect open-ended data?
Answer: Satisficing occurs when respondents give minimally acceptable answers rather than making the effort to respond thoughtfully, for example writing a few vague words or repeating the question. In open-ended items it appears as very short, generic, or off-topic responses, and it increases with survey length, low motivation, and burdensome question design. Researchers can reduce satisficing by keeping surveys short and engaging, and they should screen out empty or nonsensical answers during analysis while reporting how much data were excluded.

title: How should sample size be thought about in qualitative surveys?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should sample size be thought about in qualitative surveys?
Answer: Qualitative surveys typically recruit larger samples than interview studies, often dozens to a few hundred respondents, because each individual response is thinner and patterns must be built across the dataset. The guiding consideration is whether the dataset as a whole is rich and diverse enough to answer the research question, not statistical representativeness. Researchers should anticipate that a portion of responses will be too brief to be informative and plan recruitment accordingly.

title: Can qualitative surveys produce genuinely rich data, or are they inherently superficial?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Can qualitative surveys produce genuinely rich data, or are they inherently superficial?
Answer: Methodologists have increasingly argued that well-designed qualitative surveys can yield rich, complex data, particularly on sensitive topics where anonymity liberates disclosure and across the dataset as a whole, where breadth of perspectives becomes a form of richness. Richness in surveys is thus conceptualized differently than in interviews: it lies in the range and patterning of accounts rather than the depth of any single one. The superficiality critique holds mainly when questions are poorly designed or the mode is mismatched to the research question.

title: What issues arise when survey data are collected across multiple modes, such as online and on paper?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What issues arise when survey data are collected across multiple modes, such as online and on paper?
Answer: Different modes can produce systematically different responses: typed online answers may differ in length and candor from handwritten ones, and the populations reached by each mode often differ in age, literacy, and access. When combining modes, researchers should keep question wording and presentation as equivalent as possible, record which mode each response came from, and examine whether patterns differ by mode before pooling the data. Mode differences should be discussed as a potential influence on findings rather than ignored.

title: How does item nonresponse threaten the interpretation of open-ended survey data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Other Data Collection Methods
Subcategory: Open-ended surveys & qualitative questionnaires
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How does item nonresponse threaten the interpretation of open-ended survey data?
Answer: Respondents who skip open-ended items are rarely a random subset; those with less time, lower literacy, weaker topic engagement, or more marginalized positions are often overrepresented among non-responders. The analyzed text therefore reflects the perspectives of the more articulate and motivated, which can skew themes toward particular social groups.
