Answer: In the classic model the substantive literature review is delayed until the theory has emerged, at which point published work is treated as more data: it is compared constantly with the generated categories and woven into the write-up to show where the theory extends, contradicts, or refines existing accounts. Eisenhardt calls a similar move 'enfolding the literature'; Charmaz likewise defers the deep literature engagement but expects a critical, theoretically sophisticated dialogue with it in the final draft. The shared rationale is that literature should sharpen an emergent theory, not force preconceived concepts onto the data.

title: What is the lifeworld (Lebenswelt) in phenomenology?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Phenomenology & IPA
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the lifeworld (Lebenswelt) in phenomenology?
Answer: The lifeworld is Husserl's term for the pre-reflective world of everyday lived experience—the taken-for-granted horizon within which we perceive, act, and relate before any scientific theorizing. Phenomenology returns to the lifeworld as the ground of all meaning, insisting that scientific abstractions are secondary constructions built upon it. Qualitative phenomenological research accordingly seeks rich descriptions of how phenomena are actually lived rather than how they are theoretically modeled.

title: What are van Manen's lifeworld existentials?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Phenomenology & IPA
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are van Manen's lifeworld existentials?
Answer: Max van Manen proposes four existentials as universal themes for phenomenological reflection: lived space (spatiality), lived body (corporeality), lived time (temporality), and lived human relation (relationality or communality). They are not categories to code data into but productive lenses—asking, for instance, how an illness reshapes a person's experience of time or of their body. Because all four pervade any experience, they help the researcher interrogate a phenomenon from multiple angles without fragmenting it.

title: What is intentionality in phenomenology, and why does it matter analytically?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Phenomenology & IPA
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is intentionality in phenomenology, and why does it matter analytically?
Answer: Intentionality is the thesis, from Brentano and Husserl, that consciousness is always consciousness of something—experience is inherently directed toward objects, whether things, people, memories, or ideas. Husserl analyzed this directedness into the noema (the object as experienced) and noesis (the act of experiencing). Analytically it means the researcher should describe both what appears to the person and the how of its appearing, keeping experiencer and experienced together rather than studying either in isolation.

title: How does IPA move from single-case analysis to cross-case patterns?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Phenomenology & IPA
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How does IPA move from single-case analysis to cross-case patterns?
Answer: IPA's idiographic commitment requires analyzing each case fully on its own terms before looking across cases, and Smith and colleagues advise bracketing, as far as possible, the themes from earlier cases when starting a new one. Only after all cases are analyzed does the researcher look for patterns of convergence and divergence, developing group-level themes that capture shared qualities while preserving the particular ways each individual manifests them. Good IPA write-ups therefore show both the shared theme and the idiosyncratic voice of each participant within it.

title: What is the difference between the natural attitude and the phenomenological attitude?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Phenomenology & IPA
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is the difference between the natural attitude and the phenomenological attitude?
Answer: The natural attitude is our default, unreflective stance in which we simply take the world's existence for granted and live absorbed in practical concerns. The phenomenological attitude, achieved through the epoché, suspends that existential commitment so that attention shifts to how phenomena appear to consciousness—their modes of givenness—rather than to the objects themselves. The shift does not doubt the world but changes the register of inquiry from facts about things to the structures of experiencing them.

title: What is the biographical-narrative interview and how is it analyzed?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Narrative analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the biographical-narrative interview and how is it analyzed?
Answer: Rooted in Fritz Schütze's work and elaborated by Gabriele Rosenthal and, in Britain, Tom Wengraf's BNIM, the biographical-narrative interview opens with a single narrative-inducing question inviting the whole life story, followed by an uninterrupted main narration and only then by narrative-pointed follow-up questions. Analysis characteristically distinguishes the 'lived life' (the chronology of events) from the 'told story' (how the life is narrated), reconstructing each separately before relating them. The gap between what happened and how it is told is treated as analytically revealing of the narrator's present perspective and identity work.

title: What is an epiphany in narrative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Narrative analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an epiphany in narrative research?
Answer: Norman Denzin used 'epiphany' for turning-point moments that leave a mark on a life and alter its meaning—crises, revelations, or events after which things are never the same. Such moments often serve as the structural anchors of life stories, and narrative researchers attend to how tellers construct, place, and interpret them. Denzin distinguished forms including the major epiphany, the cumulative epiphany, the minor or illuminative epiphany, and the relived epiphany.

title: What is narrative positioning analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Narrative analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is narrative positioning analysis?
Answer: Michael Bamberg proposed analyzing positioning at three levels: how characters are positioned in relation to one another within the story world; how the narrator positions themselves interactionally toward the audience in the act of telling; and how the teller positions themselves in relation to broader cultural discourses or master narratives, thereby making identity claims. The approach links the micro-analysis of storytelling interaction with larger questions of identity and ideology. It is especially associated with the study of 'small stories' in everyday talk.

title: How can narrative genre or tone be analyzed in personal stories?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Narrative analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can narrative genre or tone be analyzed in personal stories?
Answer: Analysts can ask what cultural plot forms a story draws on—Kenneth and Mary Gergen, for instance, distinguished progressive, regressive, and stability narratives by the direction the evaluative storyline moves. Others use literary genres such as romance, comedy, tragedy, and satire, following Northrop Frye's typology, to characterize how tellers emplot their experience. Genre analysis shows that personal stories are shaped by shared narrative conventions, revealing the cultural resources available to make particular experiences tellable.

title: What is narrative smoothing and why does it matter?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Narrative analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is narrative smoothing and why does it matter?
Answer: Narrative smoothing, a term used by Donald Spence and discussed by Donald Polkinghorne, refers to the way messy, fragmentary accounts get tidied—by tellers and by researchers—into coherent, well-formed stories. Some smoothing is inevitable in producing readable research narratives, but it risks writing out contradictions, gaps, and loose ends that may be analytically important. Narrative researchers are therefore urged to notice and report incoherence rather than manufacture seamlessness, and to be transparent about their own shaping of participants' stories.

title: What is preference organization in conversation analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Discourse analysis & conversation analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is preference organization in conversation analysis?
Answer: Preference organization describes the systematic asymmetry in how alternative responses to a first action are built: preferred responses (accepting an invitation, agreeing with an assessment) are typically delivered promptly and simply, while dispreferred responses (refusals, disagreements) are marked by delays, hesitations, hedges, and accounts. The terms are structural, describing the design of turns, not the speakers' psychological desires. Analyzing preference reveals how social solidarity and face concerns are managed in the fine detail of talk.

title: What is institutional talk in conversation analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Discourse analysis & conversation analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is institutional talk in conversation analysis?
Answer: Institutional talk, studied in the program associated with Paul Drew and John Heritage, is interaction in workplaces such as clinics, courts, classrooms, and news interviews, where talk is shaped by institution-specific goals, constraints on allowable contributions, and distinctive inferential frameworks. Analysts compare institutional interaction against the baseline of ordinary conversation to show how turn-taking, question design, and other practices are specialized—for example, the interviewer-answers restriction in news interviews. The approach demonstrates how institutions are 'talked into being' through these adapted practices.

title: What is the difference between 'discourse' with a small d and 'Discourse' with a big D in James Gee's terms?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Discourse analysis & conversation analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between 'discourse' with a small d and 'Discourse' with a big D in James Gee's terms?
Answer: For Gee, small-d discourse refers to language-in-use—stretches of actual spoken or written language and how they are put together. Big-D Discourse refers to language combined with ways of acting, interacting, valuing, dressing, thinking, and using objects that together enact socially recognizable identities, such as being a doctor or a gamer. The distinction reminds analysts that meaning depends not only on linguistic form but on membership in wider social practices.

title: What is deviant case analysis in conversation analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Discourse analysis & conversation analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is deviant case analysis in conversation analysis?
Answer: Deviant case analysis is the practice of deliberately examining instances that depart from a candidate interactional pattern rather than setting them aside. Often the deviant case shows participants themselves orienting to the norm—for example, accounting for or repairing the departure—which strengthens the claim that the pattern is a normative practice rather than a statistical regularity; alternatively, the deviant case forces the analyst to revise the analysis. It is conversation analysis's principal internal validity check and reflects its commitment to accounting for every case in a collection.

title: What is multimodal analysis of discourse and interaction?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Discourse analysis & conversation analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is multimodal analysis of discourse and interaction?
Answer: Multimodal analysis extends the study of discourse beyond words to other semiotic resources: gaze, gesture, body posture, movement, and the handling of objects and space in face-to-face interaction, and image, layout, and typography in texts, as in Kress and van Leeuwen's social semiotics. In interaction studies it typically requires video data and transcription systems that align embodied conduct with talk. The rationale is that meaning is accomplished through orchestrated combinations of modes, so an audio-only or text-only analysis can miss how actions are actually built.

title: How does speech act theory inform discourse analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Discourse analysis & conversation analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How does speech act theory inform discourse analysis?
Answer: Speech act theory, from J. L. Austin and John Searle, established that utterances do not merely describe the world but perform actions—promising, requesting, apologizing, warning. Discourse analysts inherited this focus on the action orientation of language: the analytic question becomes what talk is doing in context, not just what it says. Discursive psychology in particular builds on this insight, examining how descriptions and psychological terms are deployed to manage accountability, blame, and stake in interaction.

title: What are the phases of content analysis in Elo and Kyngäs's model?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Qualitative content analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the phases of content analysis in Elo and Kyngäs's model?
Answer: Elo and Kyngäs describe three phases: preparation, in which the researcher selects the unit of analysis and immerses themselves in the data to make sense of the whole; organizing, which in the inductive route involves open coding, grouping, categorization, and abstraction, and in the deductive route involves building a categorization matrix from prior theory and coding data into it; and reporting, in which the analysis process and results are described in enough detail for readers to judge trustworthiness. Their model is widely used in nursing and health sciences. It accommodates both inductive and deductive designs within one framework.

title: How should coders handle a text segment that seems to fit more than one category?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Qualitative content analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should coders handle a text segment that seems to fit more than one category?
Answer: In Schreier's account of qualitative content analysis, categories within a single dimension of the coding frame must be mutually exclusive, so a segment can receive only one code per dimension; persistent overlap signals that category definitions or decision rules need sharpening, or that the categories belong to different dimensions. A segment may legitimately be coded under several different dimensions, since each dimension captures a distinct aspect of meaning. Documenting the decision rules used to resolve borderline cases is part of the method's claim to systematic rigor.

title: Is qualitative content analysis tied to a particular epistemology?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Qualitative content analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Is qualitative content analysis tied to a particular epistemology?
Answer: Qualitative content analysis is usually presented as epistemologically flexible: it can serve realist descriptive aims or more interpretive, constructionist projects depending on how latent meaning and context are handled. Critics note, however, that its emphasis on stable category systems, coder agreement, and sometimes frequency reporting carries residues of its quantitative, (post)positivist origins, which can sit awkwardly with strongly constructionist claims. Researchers are therefore advised to align their version of the method—and the claims they make from it—explicitly with their guiding framework.

title: How is material selected for a qualitative content analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Qualitative content analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How is material selected for a qualitative content analysis?
Answer: The researcher first defines the body of relevant material—for example, which documents, media items, or transcripts bear on the research question—and then samples purposively within it, specifying time frames, sources, and inclusion criteria. Because rich texts are analyzed intensively, feasibility matters, and selection aims at capturing the diversity of relevant material rather than statistical representativeness. Transparent reporting of what was included and excluded, and why, is essential for the credibility of the findings.

title: What is a pilot or trial coding phase in qualitative content analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Qualitative content analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is a pilot or trial coding phase in qualitative content analysis?
Answer: In Schreier's procedure, the coding frame is tried out on a portion of the material before the main analysis: two coders code the same segments independently (or one coder codes twice at an interval), the codings are compared, and discrepancies are discussed. Disagreements are used diagnostically to revise category definitions, decision rules, and examples until the frame works reliably. Only after this trial phase is the revised frame applied to the full dataset, which protects both the consistency and the validity of the analysis.

title: What is time-series analysis as a case study analytic technique?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Case study analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is time-series analysis as a case study analytic technique?
Answer: Time-series analysis, one of Yin's analytic techniques, traces how relevant events or indicators within a case change over time and compares the observed trajectory with trajectories predicted by theory or by rival explanations. Simple versions include constructing chronologies that test whether events occurred in the sequence a causal claim requires. Its strength is that temporal ordering imposes discipline on causal inference inside a single case.

title: What is a pilot case study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Case study analysis
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a pilot case study?
Answer: A pilot case study is a preliminary case Yin recommends conducting before the main data collection, used to refine the case study protocol—both the content of the questions and the field procedures. Pilot cases are often chosen for convenience, access, or geographic proximity, and inquiry there can be broader and less structured than in the eventual study. Unlike a mere pretest, the pilot can shape substantive research design decisions as well as logistics.

title: What are the case study database and the chain of evidence?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Case study analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the case study database and the chain of evidence?
Answer: Both are reliability tactics from Yin. The case study database is an organized repository of all the evidence—notes, documents, tabular materials, narratives—kept separate from the final report so other investigators can review the raw materials. The chain of evidence means a reader can trace the derivation of any conclusion backward from report to database to protocol to research questions, and forward again, much like evidence handling in a legal case.

title: What is process tracing and how does it relate to case study analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Case study analysis
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is process tracing and how does it relate to case study analysis?
Answer: Process tracing, developed in political science by Alexander George, Andrew Bennett, and later Derek Beach and Rasmus Pedersen, is a within-case method for causal inference that traces the mechanism linking cause and outcome through diagnostic pieces of evidence. Evidence is weighed with tests of differing probative value—commonly labeled straw-in-the-wind, hoop, smoking-gun, and doubly decisive—according to whether passing them is necessary and/or sufficient for a hypothesis. It complements Yin's pattern matching by specifying more formally how single-case evidence can discriminate between rival explanations.

title: What are categorical aggregation and direct interpretation in Stake's approach to case analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Analytic Approaches & Traditions
Subcategory: Case study analysis
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are categorical aggregation and direct interpretation in Stake's approach to case analysis?
Answer: Stake describes two complementary ways of reaching meaning in a case: categorical aggregation, in which the analyst collects multiple instances from the data until issue-relevant meanings emerge from the class of instances, and direct interpretation, in which a single significant instance is examined deeply and meaning is drawn from it without aggregation. Intrinsic case studies lean more on direct interpretation, instrumental ones more on aggregation. Both feed into the patterns and naturalistic generalizations that Stake sees as the products of case analysis.

title: What is trustworthiness in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is trustworthiness in qualitative research?
Answer: Trustworthiness is the overall standard by which the quality of qualitative research is judged, indicating that findings are worth paying attention to and worth acting upon. Lincoln and Guba proposed four criteria for establishing it: credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability. These serve as qualitative parallels to the quantitative concepts of internal validity, external validity, reliability, and objectivity.

title: What is credibility in Lincoln and Guba's framework?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is credibility in Lincoln and Guba's framework?
Answer: Credibility refers to confidence that the findings truthfully represent participants' experiences and the phenomenon under study. It is the qualitative parallel to internal validity and addresses the 'truth value' of the research. Techniques for building credibility include prolonged engagement, persistent observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative case analysis, and member checking.

title: What is transferability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is transferability?
Answer: Transferability is the extent to which qualitative findings can be applied to other contexts, settings, or groups, serving as the qualitative parallel to external validity or generalizability. Rather than claiming universal applicability, the researcher provides rich, thick description of the context and participants so that readers can judge whether the findings fit their own situations. The responsibility for deciding whether findings transfer rests largely with the reader, not the original researcher.

title: What is dependability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is dependability?
Answer: Dependability concerns the consistency and stability of the research process over time, and is the qualitative parallel to reliability. It asks whether the study's procedures were logical, well documented, and traceable, so that another researcher could follow the decision trail. Common strategies for demonstrating dependability include maintaining an audit trail and having an external inquiry audit of the research process.

title: What is confirmability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is confirmability?
Answer: Confirmability is the degree to which findings are grounded in the data and shaped by participants rather than by researcher bias, motivation, or interest. It is the qualitative parallel to objectivity in conventional research. Confirmability is typically established through an audit trail linking findings back to raw data, reflexive journaling, and triangulation.

title: Who developed the trustworthiness criteria most commonly used in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Who developed the trustworthiness criteria most commonly used in qualitative research?
Answer: The trustworthiness framework was developed by Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba, most influentially in their 1985 book Naturalistic Inquiry. They proposed credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability as naturalistic alternatives to the conventional criteria of internal validity, external validity, reliability, and objectivity. Their framework remains the most widely cited standard for judging qualitative rigor.

title: What is prolonged engagement?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is prolonged engagement?
Answer: Prolonged engagement means spending sufficient time in the field to learn the culture, build trust with participants, and test for misinformation or distortions. It helps the researcher move beyond first impressions and understand the context deeply enough to interpret data accurately. Lincoln and Guba identified it as a key technique for establishing credibility.

title: What is thick description and how does it support transferability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is thick description and how does it support transferability?
Answer: Thick description is a detailed, richly contextualized account of the setting, participants, interactions, and meanings observed in a study, a concept popularized in research through Clifford Geertz's work. By describing the context in depth, the researcher gives readers enough information to judge whether the findings might apply to other settings. It is therefore the primary strategy for supporting transferability in Lincoln and Guba's framework.

title: How does credibility parallel internal validity in quantitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does credibility parallel internal validity in quantitative research?
Answer: Internal validity asks whether a study's conclusions accurately reflect causal or empirical reality as measured; credibility asks the analogous question for naturalistic inquiry, namely whether the reconstructions offered by the researcher are recognizable and adequate representations of participants' realities. Lincoln and Guba deliberately framed credibility as the naturalistic counterpart to internal validity while rejecting the assumption of a single measurable reality. Thus credibility is judged by how well findings are grounded in participants' perspectives rather than by control of extraneous variables.

title: What is persistent observation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is persistent observation?
Answer: Persistent observation involves focusing in depth on the elements and characteristics most relevant to the research question, identifying what really matters in the setting and studying it in detail. While prolonged engagement provides scope, persistent observation provides depth. Together they help the researcher distinguish salient features from irrelevancies, strengthening the credibility of the findings.

title: What is peer debriefing?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is peer debriefing?
Answer: Peer debriefing is the practice of regularly discussing the research process, emerging findings, and interpretations with a disinterested colleague who plays devil's advocate. The peer probes the researcher's biases, tests working hypotheses, and challenges interpretations that may not be well supported by the data. Lincoln and Guba recommended it as a credibility technique that also helps the researcher process the emotional aspects of fieldwork.

title: How does dependability differ from the quantitative concept of reliability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does dependability differ from the quantitative concept of reliability?
Answer: Quantitative reliability assumes a stable reality and asks whether repeated measurement would yield the same results, whereas dependability accepts that qualitative settings and designs evolve and instead asks whether the research process was systematic, well documented, and defensible. Dependability is demonstrated by making the decision trail transparent, so others can see how design changes and analytic choices were made. Exact replication is not the goal; traceability and methodological consistency are.

title: What strategies can a researcher use to establish confirmability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What strategies can a researcher use to establish confirmability?
Answer: The central strategy is a confirmability audit, in which an audit trail links every finding and interpretation back to raw data such as transcripts, field notes, and memos. Reflexive journaling helps the researcher recognize and document how their assumptions may have influenced the analysis, and triangulation provides corroboration from multiple sources or methods. Together these show that conclusions are grounded in the data rather than in researcher predisposition.

title: Why is transferability considered the reader's judgment rather than the researcher's claim?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Why is transferability considered the reader's judgment rather than the researcher's claim?
Answer: Lincoln and Guba argued that the original researcher cannot know all the contexts to which findings might be applied, so they cannot legitimately specify the range of transfer. The researcher's obligation is to supply the thick description of context, participants, and conditions that allows a reader to assess similarity to their own setting. The reader, who knows the receiving context, then makes the transferability judgment.

title: What is referential adequacy?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is referential adequacy?
Answer: Referential adequacy involves setting aside a portion of the raw data during collection and not analyzing it until preliminary findings have been developed, then returning to the archived material to test whether the findings hold. It provides a benchmark against which interpretations can be checked, supporting credibility. Although proposed by Lincoln and Guba, it is used less often in practice because researchers are frequently reluctant to withhold data from analysis.

title: What are Guba and Lincoln's authenticity criteria?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What are Guba and Lincoln's authenticity criteria?
Answer: Beyond trustworthiness, Guba and Lincoln proposed authenticity criteria rooted specifically in constructivist assumptions: fairness, ontological authenticity, educative authenticity, catalytic authenticity, and tactical authenticity. Fairness requires that all stakeholder constructions be solicited and honored; the ontological and educative criteria concern whether participants' own understandings and their appreciation of others' views are enhanced; the catalytic and tactical criteria concern whether the research stimulates and empowers action. These criteria judge the study's consequences for participants, not only the accuracy of its representations.

title: What criticisms have been made of the trustworthiness framework?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What criticisms have been made of the trustworthiness framework?
Answer: Critics argue that by constructing parallels to internal validity, external validity, reliability, and objectivity, the framework remains tethered to positivist logic rather than offering genuinely interpretivist standards, a tension Lincoln and Guba themselves later acknowledged. Others contend that the criteria can be applied as a mechanical checklist, encouraging ritualistic technique-listing rather than genuine methodological reflection. A further critique is that a single universal set of criteria fits poorly with the diversity of qualitative paradigms and genres.

title: What is catalytic authenticity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is catalytic authenticity?
Answer: Catalytic authenticity is one of Guba and Lincoln's authenticity criteria for constructivist inquiry, referring to the extent to which the research stimulates and facilitates action by participants. A study high in catalytic authenticity does not merely describe a situation but energizes stakeholders to act on their circumstances. It is closely related to tactical authenticity, which concerns whether participants are actually empowered with the means to act.

title: Why did Lincoln and Guba propose parallel criteria rather than adopting conventional validity and reliability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Trustworthiness criteria
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Why did Lincoln and Guba propose parallel criteria rather than adopting conventional validity and reliability?
Answer: They argued that conventional criteria rest on positivist assumptions, including a single objective reality and researcher-subject independence, that are incompatible with naturalistic inquiry's premises of multiple constructed realities and researcher-participant interaction. Parallel criteria allowed qualitative work to be judged rigorously on its own philosophical terms while remaining intelligible to audiences trained in conventional standards. The move was strategic as well as philosophical, helping legitimize qualitative research during the paradigm debates of the 1980s.

title: Does the concept of validity apply to qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Does the concept of validity apply to qualitative research?
Answer: Yes, but it is understood differently than in quantitative research. In qualitative work, validity generally refers to whether the findings accurately and credibly represent the phenomenon and participants' meanings, rather than to measurement accuracy or statistical inference. Many qualitative researchers prefer alternative terms such as credibility or trustworthiness, while others, like Joseph Maxwell, retain the word validity but redefine it for interpretive inquiry.

title: What does reliability mean in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does reliability mean in qualitative research?
Answer: In qualitative research, reliability refers to the consistency and dependability of the research process, such as whether coding was applied consistently and whether procedures were documented clearly enough to be followed by others. It does not mean exact replicability of findings, since qualitative studies occur in unique, evolving contexts. Many researchers substitute the term dependability, following Lincoln and Guba.

title: What is inter-coder reliability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is inter-coder reliability?
Answer: Inter-coder reliability is the degree to which two or more analysts independently assign the same codes to the same data segments. It is often quantified with agreement statistics such as percentage agreement or Cohen's kappa. Its use in qualitative research is debated: it suits structured, team-based content analysis, but researchers in interpretive traditions argue that coding is an interpretive act where independent agreement is neither expected nor the best marker of quality.

title: What is descriptive validity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is descriptive validity?
Answer: Descriptive validity, a term from Joseph Maxwell's typology, refers to the factual accuracy of the researcher's account: whether what is reported as said, done, or observed actually occurred. It is the most basic form of validity in qualitative research, since interpretation depends on getting the descriptive record right. Accurate recording, verbatim transcription, and careful field notes are the main safeguards.

title: Why can qualitative findings not be judged by statistical generalizability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why can qualitative findings not be judged by statistical generalizability?
Answer: Qualitative studies use small, purposefully selected samples that are not designed to be statistically representative of a population, so probability-based inference from sample to population does not apply. Instead, qualitative research aims for other forms of generalization, such as transferability judged through thick description or analytic generalization to concepts and theory. Judging such studies by statistical generalizability applies a criterion the design never claimed to meet.

title: What is meant by rigor in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is meant by rigor in qualitative research?
Answer: Rigor refers to the thoroughness, care, and systematic quality of a study's design, data collection, analysis, and reporting. A rigorous qualitative study documents its procedures, grounds interpretations in data, addresses researcher influence, and uses recognized quality strategies such as triangulation, member checking, or audit trails. Rigor is what makes findings trustworthy rather than merely anecdotal.

title: Why do some qualitative researchers avoid the terms validity and reliability altogether?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why do some qualitative researchers avoid the terms validity and reliability altogether?
Answer: They argue that these terms carry positivist assumptions, such as a single measurable reality and the possibility of researcher neutrality, that conflict with interpretivist and constructivist paradigms. Using them risks judging qualitative work by inappropriate quantitative standards. Alternative vocabularies, most prominently Lincoln and Guba's trustworthiness criteria, were developed to express quality in terms consistent with qualitative epistemology.

title: What is a validity threat in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a validity threat in qualitative research?
Answer: A validity threat is a plausible alternative explanation for the findings or a way the researcher could be wrong, such as researcher bias shaping interpretation or reactivity, where the researcher's presence changes participants' behavior. Maxwell argues that qualitative researchers should identify the specific threats most relevant to their study and design checks against them, rather than relying on generic procedures. Strategies include triangulation, negative case analysis, rich data, and respondent validation.

title: What is Maxwell's typology of validity in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is Maxwell's typology of validity in qualitative research?
Answer: Joseph Maxwell distinguished several types of understanding at stake in qualitative research: descriptive validity (factual accuracy of the account), interpretive validity (accuracy in representing participants' meanings), and theoretical validity (the adequacy of the concepts and explanations applied to the data). He also discussed generalizability and evaluative validity as further categories. The typology helps researchers identify which kind of validity a particular threat or strategy addresses.

title: What is interpretive validity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is interpretive validity?
Answer: Interpretive validity, in Maxwell's typology, is the degree to which the researcher accurately captures participants' own meanings, intentions, and perspectives rather than imposing external interpretations. It is grounded in the participants' language and concepts, so strategies such as using verbatim quotes, in-depth probing, and member checking help support it. A study can be descriptively accurate yet interpretively invalid if it misconstrues what events meant to the people involved.

title: What is theoretical validity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is theoretical validity?
Answer: Theoretical validity refers to the adequacy of the theoretical constructs and relationships a researcher uses to explain the data, going beyond description and participant meaning to the level of explanation. It asks whether the concepts fit the phenomena and whether the postulated relationships among them are credible. Threats include forcing data into preconceived frameworks and ignoring discrepant evidence that challenges the emerging theory.

title: What is analytic generalization?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is analytic generalization?
Answer: Analytic generalization, a term associated with Robert Yin's case study methodology, is the process of generalizing from empirical findings to theory or concepts rather than from a sample to a population. A case study's results are used to support, refine, or challenge theoretical propositions, which can then be applied to other situations where the theory is relevant. It is one of the main answers to the question of how small-sample qualitative research can have broader significance.

title: Should qualitative researchers always report inter-coder agreement statistics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Should qualitative researchers always report inter-coder agreement statistics?
Answer: No; it depends on the methodology and its epistemological assumptions. Agreement statistics fit structured approaches such as qualitative content analysis or codebook-based team coding, where codes are defined precisely and applied consistently. In reflexive approaches, such as Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, coding is treated as an interpretive, researcher-subjective process, and the authors explicitly argue that inter-rater reliability is inappropriate because it assumes coding aims at consensus on a single correct coding.

title: What did LeCompte and Goetz mean by internal and external reliability in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What did LeCompte and Goetz mean by internal and external reliability in qualitative research?
Answer: LeCompte and Goetz adapted reliability language for ethnography: external reliability concerns whether independent researchers would discover the same phenomena or generate the same constructs in the same or similar settings, while internal reliability concerns whether multiple observers within a study would agree in their descriptions and codings. They acknowledged that exact replication is effectively impossible in naturalistic settings, so reliability is approximated through explicit documentation of researcher role, informant choice, context, and methods. Their framework was an early attempt to translate conventional criteria for qualitative fieldwork.

title: What is evaluative validity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is evaluative validity?
Answer: Evaluative validity, the final category in Maxwell's typology, concerns the legitimacy of evaluative judgments the researcher makes about the actions or situations studied, such as calling a practice harmful or unjust. It differs from descriptive, interpretive, and theoretical validity because it applies an evaluative framework to the data rather than describing or explaining it. Maxwell notes it is less central to most qualitative studies but becomes important in critical and evaluative research.

title: How can qualitative researchers address concerns about replication?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can qualitative researchers address concerns about replication?
Answer: Since identical replication of a naturalistic study is impossible, qualitative researchers address the underlying concern, arbitrariness, through transparency: documenting sampling decisions, data collection procedures, coding frames, and analytic steps in an audit trail. This allows others to follow and evaluate the decision path, and to conduct conceptual replications in comparable settings. The goal shifts from reproducing identical results to demonstrating that the process was systematic and the conclusions well grounded.

title: What is Kvale's notion of validation as craftsmanship?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is Kvale's notion of validation as craftsmanship?
Answer: Steinar Kvale argued that validity in qualitative interviewing is not a final stamp applied at the end but a quality of craftsmanship exercised throughout the research: continually checking, questioning, and theoretically interpreting the findings. He complemented this with communicative validity, where the soundness of knowledge claims is tested in dialogue with participants and the research community, and pragmatic validity, where claims are judged by their usefulness for action. Validation thus becomes an ongoing practice embedded in the entire research process.

title: What is catalytic validity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is catalytic validity?
Answer: Catalytic validity, a concept articulated by Patti Lather within critical research, is the degree to which a study reorients, energizes, and empowers participants to understand and transform their own social reality. It reflects an emancipatory view of research in which quality is judged partly by the change the inquiry generates, not only by the accuracy of its representations. The idea parallels Guba and Lincoln's catalytic authenticity and is central to participatory and action research traditions.

title: How have postmodern and poststructural researchers reconceptualized validity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How have postmodern and poststructural researchers reconceptualized validity?
Answer: Postmodern scholars question whether any criteria can guarantee correspondence between an account and reality, since all accounts are partial, situated, and constructed through language. Writers such as Patti Lather have proposed transgressive reconceptualizations of validity that embrace multiplicity, self-reflexivity, and the problematizing of authority rather than seeking certainty. In this view, validity becomes an ongoing, unsettled practice of interrogating how knowledge claims are produced, rather than a checklist to be satisfied.

title: What is Hammersley's subtle realism and what does it imply for judging qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Validity & reliability debates
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is Hammersley's subtle realism and what does it imply for judging qualitative research?
Answer: Martyn Hammersley's subtle realism holds that an independent reality exists but that we can never know it with certainty; all knowledge is a human construction judged by its plausibility and credibility given the evidence. This position rejects both naive realism and radical relativism, implying that qualitative accounts should be assessed by whether their claims are sufficiently supported, not by whether they perfectly reproduce reality. Quality assessment therefore focuses on the strength of evidence relative to the centrality and extraordinariness of the claim.

title: What are Denzin's four types of triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What are Denzin's four types of triangulation?
Answer: Norman Denzin distinguished four types: data triangulation (multiple sources, times, places, or people), investigator triangulation (multiple researchers), theory triangulation (multiple theoretical perspectives), and methodological triangulation (multiple methods of data collection). This typology remains the standard way of classifying triangulation strategies. Studies may combine several types to strengthen their findings.

title: What is data triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is data triangulation?
Answer: Data triangulation involves gathering data on the same phenomenon from multiple sources, such as different participants, sites, or time points. For example, a study of workplace culture might interview managers, frontline staff, and clients, or observe the same team at different times. Comparing these sources can corroborate findings and reveal how perspectives vary across positions and contexts.

title: What is methodological triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is methodological triangulation?
Answer: Methodological triangulation is the use of more than one data collection method to study the same phenomenon, such as combining interviews with observation or document analysis. Each method has distinct strengths and blind spots, so combining them can offset individual weaknesses and provide a more complete picture. Denzin further distinguished within-method triangulation (varieties of one method) from between-method triangulation (different methods).

title: What is investigator triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is investigator triangulation?
Answer: Investigator triangulation involves multiple researchers collecting or analyzing the data, then comparing their observations and interpretations. Discussing points of agreement and disagreement can expose individual blind spots and idiosyncratic readings of the data. It is common in team-based studies, where co-coding and analytic meetings serve this function.

title: What is theory triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is theory triangulation?
Answer: Theory triangulation means examining the same data through more than one theoretical lens or set of hypotheses. For instance, interview data on organizational change might be interpreted through both an institutional theory lens and a sensemaking lens. Comparing what each perspective illuminates and obscures deepens interpretation and guards against the limits of a single framework.

title: Why do qualitative researchers use triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why do qualitative researchers use triangulation?
Answer: Researchers use triangulation for two main purposes: corroboration, where converging evidence from different sources or methods increases confidence in a finding, and completeness, where different perspectives together produce a richer, more comprehensive understanding. It is also one of Lincoln and Guba's recommended techniques for establishing credibility. Even when sources diverge, exploring the divergence often generates important insight.

title: What is an example of triangulation in an interview study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an example of triangulation in an interview study?
Answer: A researcher studying nurses' experiences of understaffing might interview nurses, observe shifts on the ward, and analyze internal staffing documents. If the interviews describe rushed handovers, the observations show them happening, and the documents record vacancy rates, the finding is corroborated across three sources. Discrepancies among the sources would themselves become analytically interesting, prompting further inquiry.

title: Does triangulation guarantee more valid findings?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Does triangulation guarantee more valid findings?
Answer: No. Triangulation can strengthen confidence, but convergence does not prove correctness, since multiple sources or methods can share the same bias, and divergence does not prove error, since different methods may legitimately capture different facets of a phenomenon. Methodologists therefore caution against treating triangulation as a simple validity test and encourage using it to deepen and complicate understanding as well as to corroborate.

title: What is the difference between within-method and between-method triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between within-method and between-method triangulation?
Answer: Within-method triangulation uses multiple varieties or strategies inside a single method, such as combining different question formats and scales within interviewing, or multiple observation points within an observational study. Between-method triangulation combines fundamentally different methods, such as interviews plus document analysis plus observation. Between-method triangulation is generally considered stronger because the methods' weaknesses are less likely to overlap.

title: How should a researcher handle contradictory findings from triangulated sources?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should a researcher handle contradictory findings from triangulated sources?
Answer: Contradictions should be treated as data, not as failure. The researcher examines why sources diverge: the methods may tap different aspects of the phenomenon, participants may present themselves differently in different situations, or one source may be less dependable in this context. Reporting and interpreting the divergence often produces a more nuanced account than forced convergence would, for example revealing gaps between what people say and what they do.

title: What is the difference between using triangulation for confirmation and for completeness?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between using triangulation for confirmation and for completeness?
Answer: Triangulation for confirmation seeks convergence: independent sources or methods pointing to the same conclusion increase confidence that the finding is not an artifact of one method. Triangulation for completeness seeks comprehensiveness: different sources illuminate different facets of a complex phenomenon, and together they build a fuller picture even without convergence. Being explicit about which purpose is intended clarifies how divergent results should be interpreted.

title: What are the dimensions of data triangulation in Denzin's scheme?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the dimensions of data triangulation in Denzin's scheme?
Answer: Denzin subdivided data triangulation into three dimensions: time, space, and person. Time triangulation collects data at different times or stages; space triangulation collects data in different settings or sites; person triangulation collects data from different individuals or levels, such as individuals, groups, and collectives. Varying these dimensions tests whether findings hold across occasions, places, and perspectives.

title: How is triangulation used in case study research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How is triangulation used in case study research?
Answer: Case study methodology relies heavily on triangulation because a case is understood through multiple types of evidence, such as interviews, documents, archival records, observations, and physical artifacts. Robert Yin identifies the use of multiple sources of evidence, converging on the same facts, as a key tactic for strengthening construct validity in case studies. Maintaining a chain of evidence from questions to data to conclusions complements this triangulation.

title: How does triangulation relate to mixed methods research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does triangulation relate to mixed methods research?
Answer: Triangulation was one of the original rationales for mixed methods designs: combining qualitative and quantitative approaches so their results could be compared for convergence on the same question. Mixed methods scholarship now distinguishes triangulation from other purposes of mixing, such as complementarity, development, and expansion. In a triangulation or convergent design, qualitative and quantitative strands are collected in parallel and their findings are merged and compared.

title: What are practical challenges of implementing triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are practical challenges of implementing triangulation?
Answer: Triangulation multiplies the time, cost, and expertise required, since each additional method or source demands its own competent design, collection, and analysis. Integrating disparate data types is analytically demanding, and poorly executed additional methods can weaken rather than strengthen a study. Researchers must also plan how they will compare and reconcile findings across sources before the data arrive, or the comparison risks becoming ad hoc.

title: Can triangulation be used within the analysis stage rather than data collection?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Can triangulation be used within the analysis stage rather than data collection?
Answer: Yes. Investigator triangulation often occurs at analysis, when multiple researchers independently code or interpret the same data and then compare their readings, and theory triangulation applies different conceptual lenses to the same dataset. Analysts may also triangulate analytic techniques, for example comparing the results of thematic analysis with a matrix-based or narrative analysis of the same material. These strategies test whether conclusions depend on one analyst or one analytic route.

title: What epistemological critiques have been raised against triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What epistemological critiques have been raised against triangulation?
Answer: Critics argue that the corroboration logic of triangulation presupposes a single fixed reality on which methods can converge, an assumption at odds with constructivist views that different methods constitute phenomena differently rather than viewing one object from different angles. From this perspective, interviews and observations do not measure the same thing twice; they produce different situated accounts. Such critics favor treating multiple methods as generating complementary or intersecting perspectives rather than as validity checks.

title: What is crystallization and how does it differ from triangulation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is crystallization and how does it differ from triangulation?
Answer: Crystallization, proposed by Laurel Richardson, replaces the rigid two-dimensional imagery of the triangle with the crystal, which reflects and refracts light differently from every angle. It embraces the idea that there are more than three sides to any account and that what we see depends on our angle of repose, combining multiple genres of representation and analysis without expecting them to converge on one truth. Where triangulation often implies validation through convergence, crystallization foregrounds partiality, multiplicity, and deepened complexity.

title: Is divergence between triangulated methods a sign of research failure?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Is divergence between triangulated methods a sign of research failure?
Answer: No; methodologists increasingly treat divergence as an analytic opportunity rather than a defect. Different methods can legitimately access different layers of a phenomenon, such as public accounts versus enacted practice, so inconsistency may reveal genuine complexity, context dependence, or impression management. The researcher's task is to theorize the divergence, which frequently yields more sophisticated conclusions than simple convergence would.

title: How does investigator triangulation differ from inter-coder reliability testing?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Triangulation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How does investigator triangulation differ from inter-coder reliability testing?
Answer: Inter-coder reliability testing quantifies the degree of independent agreement between coders applying a fixed coding scheme, treating agreement as the goal. Investigator triangulation uses multiple researchers to enrich interpretation: disagreements are explored through discussion to expose assumptions and generate deeper readings, not merely resolved to raise an agreement statistic. The former reflects a measurement logic, the latter an interpretive logic in which multiple perspectives add analytic value.

title: What is member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is member checking?
Answer: Member checking, also called respondent validation, is the practice of returning data, analyses, or interpretations to participants so they can assess accuracy and resonance with their experiences. It can involve reviewing interview transcripts, summaries, or draft findings. Lincoln and Guba described it as a key technique for establishing credibility in qualitative research.

title: Why do researchers use member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why do researchers use member checking?
Answer: Member checking gives participants an opportunity to correct factual errors, clarify intentions, and challenge interpretations they consider wrong, which helps ensure the account represents their perspectives fairly. It can also surface additional information as participants elaborate on earlier statements. Beyond accuracy, it reflects a respectful, participatory stance toward the people whose experiences the research represents.

title: At what stages of a study can member checking occur?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: At what stages of a study can member checking occur?
Answer: Member checking can happen during data collection, when the interviewer summarizes and reflects back what a participant has said to confirm understanding; after transcription, when participants review their transcripts; and after analysis, when participants comment on summaries, themes, or draft reports. Each stage checks something different, from descriptive accuracy to interpretive adequacy. Researchers should specify which form they used rather than claiming member checking generically.

title: What is transcript verification?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is transcript verification?
Answer: Transcript verification is a basic form of member checking in which participants receive their interview transcript and confirm that it accurately records what they said, sometimes correcting errors or adding clarifications. It addresses descriptive accuracy rather than the researcher's interpretation. Its value is debated, since participants rarely make substantive changes and transcripts of natural speech can be uncomfortable to read, but it can build trust and catch factual mistakes.

title: Is member checking required in every qualitative study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Is member checking required in every qualitative study?
Answer: No. Member checking is one credibility strategy among many, and its appropriateness depends on the methodology, the research question, and practical and ethical circumstances. Some designs, such as certain discourse-analytic or theory-driven studies, interpret data at a level participants would not be expected to validate, and some populations are hard or inappropriate to re-contact. What matters is choosing quality strategies that fit the study and justifying that choice.

title: What materials can be shared with participants during member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What materials can be shared with participants during member checking?
Answer: Depending on the design, researchers may share full transcripts, interview summaries, case descriptions, preliminary themes, or draft sections of the final report. Sharing accessible summaries rather than raw academic analysis often produces more meaningful feedback. Whatever is shared must be prepared with confidentiality in mind, especially in group settings where one participant should not see another's identifiable data.

title: What is the difference between member checking and a follow-up interview?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between member checking and a follow-up interview?
Answer: A follow-up interview collects new data by exploring topics further, while member checking asks participants to evaluate existing data or interpretations for accuracy and resonance. In practice the two can be combined, since participants often elaborate while validating, and the checking session itself generates analyzable data. The distinction lies in purpose: validation of the researcher's account versus generation of additional material.

title: How did Lincoln and Guba view the importance of member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How did Lincoln and Guba view the importance of member checking?
Answer: Lincoln and Guba regarded member checking as the most crucial technique for establishing credibility, because in naturalistic inquiry the realities being represented are the participants' own constructions. If findings are to be credible, the people whose realities they claim to represent should recognize them as adequate. Later methodologists have qualified this strong claim, but it explains the technique's prominence in qualitative quality frameworks.

title: What is the difference between checking transcripts and checking interpretations?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between checking transcripts and checking interpretations?
Answer: Checking transcripts tests descriptive accuracy: did the record capture what was said. Checking interpretations tests whether the researcher's synthesis, themes, or conclusions ring true to participants' experiences, which is a more demanding and more informative form of validation. The two address different validity questions, and feedback on interpretation requires presenting analysis in a form participants can meaningfully evaluate.

title: What should a researcher do when participants disagree with the interpretation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What should a researcher do when participants disagree with the interpretation?
Answer: Disagreement should be documented and treated as data, prompting the researcher to re-examine the evidence for the contested interpretation. Sometimes the analysis is revised; sometimes the researcher retains it with a reasoned justification, reporting the disagreement transparently, because participant endorsement is not the sole arbiter of analytic adequacy, particularly for theorized or critical interpretations. The key is to take disagreement seriously without treating participants' views as an automatic veto or the researcher's view as automatically correct.

title: What are the main limitations of member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the main limitations of member checking?
Answer: Participants may lack interest, time, or the analytic frame to evaluate interpretations; they may defer to the researcher's authority or, conversely, want unflattering but accurate material removed. Accounts can change over time, so a later disagreement does not necessarily invalidate the original data. Aggregated, theorized findings may also be unrecognizable at the individual level, which limits what participant confirmation can establish.

title: What ethical risks can member checking create for participants?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What ethical risks can member checking create for participants?
Answer: Reading one's own transcript or a researcher's interpretation can be distressing, especially for sensitive topics such as illness, trauma, or bereavement, and participants may feel exposed by how they appear on paper. Re-contacting participants can also breach privacy if circumstances have changed, for example if others now have access to their mail or devices. Researchers should plan consent for re-contact, prepare participants for what reviewing material may feel like, and provide support options.

title: What is synthesized member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is synthesized member checking?
Answer: Synthesized member checking is a structured approach in which researchers return synthesized analyzed data, such as emerging themes illustrated with quotes, to participants, who comment on whether the synthesis resonates with their experience and may add further data. It was developed to make member checking of analysis more rigorous and reportable than informal transcript return. The participant responses are themselves integrated into the analysis, closing the loop between validation and interpretation.

title: How can member checking be conducted after focus group research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can member checking be conducted after focus group research?
Answer: Because focus group data are co-produced by the group, researchers typically return a summary of the group discussion or the cross-group themes rather than a full transcript, protecting each participant's contributions from exposure to others. Checking can be done individually, by sending each participant a de-identified summary for comment, or collectively in a follow-up group session. Confidentiality is the central design constraint, since participants should not receive material that identifies what specific others said.

title: How should member checking be documented and reported?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should member checking be documented and reported?
Answer: Researchers should report what was returned to participants, at what stage, how many participants responded, what feedback was received, and how that feedback changed or did not change the analysis. Vague statements that member checking was performed provide little assurance of rigor. Documenting the process in the audit trail, including disagreements and their resolution, allows readers to judge what the validation actually established.

title: How do low response rates affect the value of member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How do low response rates affect the value of member checking?
