Answer: If only a few participants respond, their feedback cannot be read as validation by the sample as a whole, and respondents may differ systematically from non-respondents, for example being more engaged or more positive. Researchers should report response rates honestly, treat feedback as additional data rather than blanket confirmation, and avoid claiming that findings were validated by participants when most did not reply. Building the check into an already-scheduled contact point can improve participation.

title: What epistemological problems have been raised about member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What epistemological problems have been raised about member checking?
Answer: Critics note that member checking assumes participants are the final authority on the meaning of their experience, yet accounts are situated and shifting, so agreement at one moment does not fix truth, and disagreement may reflect changed circumstances, self-presentation, or discomfort rather than researcher error. There is also a level-of-analysis problem: theorized, aggregated findings are not simply restatements of individual accounts, so individual endorsement is neither necessary nor sufficient for their adequacy. Consequently, many methodologists treat member checking as generating further data and demonstrating respect rather than as a definitive verification procedure.

title: How do power dynamics complicate member checking?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How do power dynamics complicate member checking?
Answer: Participants may defer to the researcher's perceived expertise and approve interpretations they privately doubt, especially where status, education, or dependence on services creates asymmetry; conversely, powerful participants such as elites or gatekeepers may pressure researchers to soften critical findings. The feedback obtained is therefore shaped by the relationship, not just by the accuracy of the analysis. Researchers can mitigate this by inviting critique explicitly, using anonymous feedback channels, and reflecting on how the relationship may have shaped responses.

title: When can member checking conflict with critical or theorized interpretation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: When can member checking conflict with critical or theorized interpretation?
Answer: Critical, psychoanalytic, and discourse-analytic approaches often interpret data in terms participants would not use, for example identifying ideology, discursive positioning, or unacknowledged assumptions, and participants may reasonably reject such readings without those readings being wrong. In these traditions, participant agreement is not the criterion of validity; the warrant lies in the coherence of the analysis and its grounding in the data. Researchers should still consider sharing findings for ethical reasons, but they must distinguish ethical accountability from epistemic validation.

title: What special considerations apply when member checking with vulnerable participants?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Member checking & respondent validation
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What special considerations apply when member checking with vulnerable participants?
Answer: Re-contacting vulnerable participants can reopen distressing topics, reveal study participation to others in their household or institution, or burden people with limited capacity or resources. Materials must be accessible, given possible literacy, language, or cognitive constraints, and the process should be optional, gently framed, and supported, for example with a choice of verbal rather than written review. Ethics protocols should specify re-contact procedures in advance, and researchers should weigh whether the credibility benefit justifies the burden in each case.

title: What is positionality?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is positionality?
Answer: Positionality refers to the researcher's social location and standpoint, including characteristics such as gender, age, class, ethnicity, professional role, and personal history, in relation to the topic and the participants. Positionality shapes access, rapport, what participants disclose, and how the researcher interprets data. Articulating one's positionality is a core reflexive practice in qualitative research.

title: What is a reflexive journal?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a reflexive journal?
Answer: A reflexive journal is a regular record in which the researcher documents personal reactions, assumptions, decisions, and evolving interpretations throughout the study. Lincoln and Guba recommended it as a technique supporting confirmability, since it creates a trace of how the researcher's perspective may have influenced the work. Entries typically cover methodological choices, emotional responses to fieldwork, and shifting understandings of the data.

title: What is bracketing?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is bracketing?
Answer: Bracketing, rooted in Husserl's phenomenology and known there as epoche, is the practice of identifying and setting aside one's preconceptions and prior knowledge about a phenomenon in order to approach participants' descriptions freshly. In research practice it involves articulating assumptions, often in writing or through interviews with a peer, so they can be held in check during data collection and analysis. It is most associated with descriptive phenomenology, though the idea of surfacing assumptions is used more widely.

title: Why does reflexivity matter for research quality?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why does reflexivity matter for research quality?
Answer: Because the qualitative researcher is the instrument through which data are generated and interpreted, unexamined assumptions can silently steer questions, interactions, and conclusions. Reflexivity makes this influence visible, enabling the researcher to check it and readers to evaluate it, which supports confirmability and interpretive honesty. It converts subjectivity from a hidden liability into an examined, reported part of the method.

title: Are qualitative researchers expected to be objective?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Are qualitative researchers expected to be objective?
Answer: Qualitative research generally rejects the ideal of the detached, objective observer, holding instead that all knowledge is produced from a perspective. The expectation is not objectivity but disciplined subjectivity: researchers acknowledge their standpoint, reflect systematically on its influence, and ground claims transparently in data. Quality is judged by this openness and rigor rather than by claims of neutrality.

title: What is the difference between personal and epistemological reflexivity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between personal and epistemological reflexivity?
Answer: Personal reflexivity concerns how the researcher's own identities, values, experiences, and life circumstances shape the research and how the research in turn affects the researcher. Epistemological reflexivity concerns how the study's assumptions, research questions, design, and analytic methods have constructed the findings, asking what the chosen approach made visible and what it excluded. Both are needed: one interrogates the person, the other interrogates the knowledge-making apparatus.

title: How does reflexivity support confirmability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does reflexivity support confirmability?
Answer: Confirmability requires showing that findings derive from the data rather than researcher predisposition, and reflexivity provides the mechanism for tracking and disclosing that predisposition. A reflexive journal documents assumptions, reactions, and decision points, which can be included in the audit trail and examined during a confirmability audit. By making the researcher's influence explicit, reflexivity lets readers and auditors judge whether interpretations are data-grounded.

title: What are the advantages and risks of insider research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the advantages and risks of insider research?
Answer: Insiders often enjoy quicker access, greater trust, shared language, and contextual knowledge that helps them ask pertinent questions and interpret nuance. The risks include over-identification with participants, assuming shared meaning without probing, difficulty seeing routine practices as noteworthy, and role conflicts, for example when a colleague-researcher hears about wrongdoing. Deliberate reflexivity, peer debriefing, and explicit probing of the taken-for-granted are the standard countermeasures.

title: How can researchers practice reflexivity throughout a project rather than only in a final statement?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can researchers practice reflexivity throughout a project rather than only in a final statement?
Answer: Ongoing practices include keeping a reflexive journal from the design stage onward, writing memos that record analytic decisions and personal reactions, holding regular peer debriefings, and revisiting assumptions when surprises or discomfort arise in the field. Reflexive questions can be built into each stage: why this question, why these participants, why this reading of the data. A concluding positionality statement then summarizes an actual practice rather than performing one retrospectively.

title: How does bracketing differ between descriptive and interpretive phenomenology?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does bracketing differ between descriptive and interpretive phenomenology?
Answer: Descriptive phenomenology, following Husserl, treats bracketing as central: the researcher strives to suspend prior knowledge and theory to describe the phenomenon as it presents itself. Interpretive or hermeneutic phenomenology, following Heidegger and Gadamer, holds that pre-understanding cannot be fully suspended and is in fact the condition for interpretation, so instead of bracketing, researchers make their fore-conceptions explicit and use them dialogically in the hermeneutic circle. The choice reflects deep differences about whether presuppositionless description is possible.

title: How should reflexivity be written into a research report?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should reflexivity be written into a research report?
Answer: Reflexivity should appear as substantive analysis, not ritual disclosure: researchers describe their relevant positioning, give concrete examples of how it shaped access, data, or interpretation, and explain what they did in response. This may be woven through the methods and findings, for instance noting where the researcher's role visibly influenced an interview exchange. Journals increasingly expect such accounts, and checklists like COREQ include items on the researcher's characteristics and relationship with participants.

title: What does reflexivity look like in a research team?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What does reflexivity look like in a research team?
Answer: Team reflexivity extends individual self-examination to the group: members compare their differing positionalities and interpretations, examine how team hierarchy shapes whose readings prevail, and document analytic decisions collectively. Practices include reflexive team meetings, exchanging memos, co-coding with discussion of divergences, and recording how disagreements were resolved. Diversity within a team can be an analytic resource when differences are explored rather than suppressed.

title: What is meant by the space between insider and outsider positions?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is meant by the space between insider and outsider positions?
Answer: Scholars argue that researchers rarely occupy a pure insider or outsider position; instead they move within a space between, being similar to participants in some respects and different in others, with the balance shifting across topics, relationships, and moments in fieldwork. A researcher who shares a profession with participants may still differ in seniority, gender, or life experience, and rapport can shift within a single interview. Recognizing this fluidity encourages continuous reflexivity about how one is positioned at each point rather than a one-time declaration.

title: What critiques have been made of reflexivity as commonly practiced?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What critiques have been made of reflexivity as commonly practiced?
Answer: Critics argue that reflexivity can degenerate into confessional self-absorption or navel-gazing that centers the researcher rather than the participants, and that ritualized positionality statements can serve as rhetorical absolution, listing identities without analyzing their actual effects on the research. Others note that researchers have limited access to their own unconscious assumptions, so self-report is an incomplete corrective. The remedy proposed is analytic reflexivity, showing concretely how positioning shaped specific data and interpretations, rather than mere disclosure.

title: How does an intersectional perspective complicate positionality?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How does an intersectional perspective complicate positionality?
Answer: Intersectionality holds that social positions such as gender, race, class, and profession operate jointly rather than additively, so a researcher's relation to participants cannot be captured by single categories. A researcher may be an insider on one axis and an outsider on another, and the salience of each axis varies by participant and moment, producing shifting configurations of power and rapport. Intersectional reflexivity therefore attends to these interacting positions and to how they pattern access, disclosure, and interpretation across the study.

title: Is complete bracketing of researcher assumptions achievable?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Is complete bracketing of researcher assumptions achievable?
Answer: Most contemporary methodologists say no: hermeneutic philosophers argue that pre-understanding is the very condition of understanding, and psychological work suggests many assumptions are not consciously accessible, so they cannot simply be set aside. Bracketing is therefore best understood as an aspirational discipline of surfacing, articulating, and monitoring assumptions rather than eliminating them. The practical implication is continuous reflexive vigilance, often aided by journaling, bracketing interviews, and peer challenge, instead of a one-time purification.

title: How can researchers prevent positionality statements from becoming performative?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Reflexivity & positionality
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How can researchers prevent positionality statements from becoming performative?
Answer: The test is analytic consequence: a non-performative statement links each disclosed position to specific, evidenced effects on the research, such as how shared background shaped what participants disclosed or how an assumption was revised when data contradicted it. Researchers can ground statements in their reflexive journal, report concrete episodes rather than abstract identity lists, and include what remained invisible to them or was pointed out by others. Disclosure without demonstrated bearing on method or interpretation is decoration, not reflexivity.

title: What is an audit trail in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an audit trail in qualitative research?
Answer: An audit trail is a systematic record of the research process, including raw data, data reduction and analysis products, coding decisions, memos, and notes on methodological choices. It allows an outsider, or the researchers themselves, to trace how conclusions were reached from the original data. Lincoln and Guba identified the audit trail as the foundation for establishing dependability and confirmability.

title: What kinds of materials belong in an audit trail?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What kinds of materials belong in an audit trail?
Answer: Typical contents include raw data such as recordings, transcripts, and field notes; analytic products such as codebooks, category definitions, and theme development notes; process documents such as memos, meeting notes, and decision logs; and reflexive materials such as the researcher's journal. Instrument development notes and successive drafts of interpretations are also valuable. Together these materials document both what was found and how.

title: Why is transparency important in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why is transparency important in qualitative research?
Answer: Transparency lets readers, reviewers, and auditors evaluate whether the methods were appropriate and the conclusions are grounded in the data, which is essential because qualitative analysis involves interpretive judgment. Clear reporting of sampling, data collection, and analytic procedures replaces blind trust with assessable evidence of rigor. Transparency also enables others to learn from, build on, and critique the work.

title: What is an inquiry audit?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an inquiry audit?
Answer: An inquiry audit is an examination of a study's process and products by a researcher not involved in the project, analogous to a fiscal audit. The auditor reviews the audit trail to assess whether the process was dependable and whether findings, interpretations, and conclusions are supported by the data. Lincoln and Guba proposed it as the principal technique for establishing dependability and confirmability.

title: What is a codebook and why does it support transparency?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a codebook and why does it support transparency?
Answer: A codebook is a structured record of the codes used in analysis, typically listing each code's label, definition, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and example data excerpts. It makes the analytic scheme explicit, supports consistent application across coders and over time, and documents how the scheme evolved. Including or describing the codebook in reports or supplements lets readers see how raw data were categorized.

title: What role do memos play in documenting analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What role do memos play in documenting analysis?
Answer: Memos are written records of the researcher's thinking during analysis, capturing ideas about codes, emerging patterns, puzzles, and decisions as they occur. They preserve the reasoning behind analytic moves that would otherwise be invisible, forming a core part of the audit trail. In grounded theory, memo-writing is treated as an essential analytic activity, not just documentation.

title: What is COREQ?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is COREQ?
Answer: COREQ, the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research, is a 32-item checklist for reporting studies using interviews and focus groups. Its items cover the research team and reflexivity, study design, and analysis and findings, prompting authors to report details such as interviewer characteristics, sampling, data saturation, and coding procedures. Many health-related journals require or encourage its use to improve reporting transparency.

title: What is a decision trail?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a decision trail?
Answer: A decision trail is the documented sequence of methodological and analytic decisions made across a study, including what was decided, when, and why, such as changes to the interview guide, sampling adjustments, or the merging of codes. It is a core component of the audit trail and the main evidence for dependability. A clear decision trail allows others to follow the logic of the study even though its naturalistic design evolved.

title: How does an audit trail support dependability and confirmability?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How does an audit trail support dependability and confirmability?
Answer: Dependability is demonstrated when the audit trail shows a logical, traceable, well-documented process, allowing an auditor to confirm that design changes and procedures were reasonable. Confirmability is demonstrated when the trail links each finding back to specific raw data, showing that interpretations are grounded in participants' words rather than researcher predisposition. The same documentation thus serves both criteria, examined from process and product angles respectively.

title: What does an external auditor actually examine during an inquiry audit?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What does an external auditor actually examine during an inquiry audit?
Answer: The auditor reviews the trail from raw data through analysis to conclusions: whether sampling and data collection followed a defensible logic, whether codes and themes are supported by the underlying excerpts, whether negative cases were considered, and whether the reflexive record shows awareness of researcher influence. The auditor then attests to the dependability of the process and the confirmability of the products. Practical audits range from full formal reviews to targeted checks of key interpretive links.

title: How should evolving codebooks be documented over the course of analysis?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should evolving codebooks be documented over the course of analysis?
Answer: Researchers should preserve dated versions of the codebook as codes are added, split, merged, redefined, or retired, along with brief notes explaining each change. This versioning shows that the final scheme emerged through systematic engagement with the data rather than arbitrary revision. Qualitative data analysis software makes this easier by logging coding structures, and the version history becomes part of the audit trail.

title: What is SRQR and how does it differ from COREQ?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is SRQR and how does it differ from COREQ?
Answer: SRQR, the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research, is a 21-item reporting guideline applicable to the full range of qualitative approaches, covering title, problem formulation, researcher characteristics, methods, findings, and integration with prior work. COREQ is narrower, designed specifically for interview and focus group studies, with detailed items about the interviewing process. Authors typically choose the checklist matching their design, with SRQR serving as the more general-purpose standard.

title: How can qualitative data analysis software support the audit trail?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can qualitative data analysis software support the audit trail?
Answer: Programs such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti, and MAXQDA store data, codes, memos, and queries in one project file, time-stamp analytic actions, and allow retrieval of every excerpt behind a code or theme. This creates an inspectable chain from raw data to findings and simplifies producing codebook versions and coding summaries for auditors or reviewers. The software documents the process but does not substitute for the researcher's own decision log and reflexive record.

title: How much procedural detail should a qualitative report include?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How much procedural detail should a qualitative report include?
Answer: Enough for readers to understand and evaluate what was actually done: who was sampled and how, how data were generated, how analysis moved from data to findings, and what quality strategies were used, including deviations and design changes. Word limits often force selectivity, so supplementary materials such as interview guides and codebooks are increasingly used. The benchmark is that a knowledgeable reader could judge the study's dependability without access to private information about participants.

title: What is a chain of evidence in case study research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is a chain of evidence in case study research?
Answer: A chain of evidence, emphasized by Robert Yin, is an explicit, traceable link from the research questions to the case study protocol, from the protocol to the collected evidence in the case database, and from that evidence to the conclusions in the report. An external observer should be able to follow the derivation in either direction. Maintaining this chain increases construct validity and the overall reliability of the case study.

title: How can researchers demonstrate the link between data and themes in a report?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can researchers demonstrate the link between data and themes in a report?
Answer: Common devices include verbatim quotations attributed to de-identified participants for each theme, tables mapping themes to example excerpts and supporting participants, and figures showing how codes were grouped into themes. Some authors include an analysis exemplar tracing one theme from raw excerpts through codes to final formulation. These displays let readers verify that themes are grounded in data rather than asserted.

title: What tensions exist between transparency and confidentiality in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What tensions exist between transparency and confidentiality in qualitative research?
Answer: Full transparency ideally includes access to raw data, yet transcripts and field notes are rich in contextual detail that can identify participants even after names are removed, especially in small or distinctive communities. Researchers must balance openness with their confidentiality promises, using strategies such as sharing redacted excerpts, detailed methods documentation instead of full data, controlled-access archives, or consent processes that explicitly cover data sharing. When the two obligations conflict, protection of participants takes precedence over openness.

title: What are the main positions in the debate over open qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What are the main positions in the debate over open qualitative data?
Answer: Proponents argue that sharing data enables verification, secondary analysis, and efficient use of participants' contributions, aligning qualitative work with open science norms. Skeptics counter that qualitative data are co-constructed in specific relationships and consent contexts, that de-identification of rich data is often impossible without destroying its meaning, and that reanalysis divorced from context risks misinterpretation. Middle positions favor tiered solutions: controlled-access repositories, sharing instruments and codebooks rather than transcripts, and consent designed for sharing from the outset.

title: Can an audit truly verify interpretive conclusions?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Can an audit truly verify interpretive conclusions?
Answer: An audit can verify that procedures were followed, decisions were documented, and interpretations are plausibly linked to data, but it cannot certify that a given interpretation is the uniquely correct one, since qualitative analysis admits multiple defensible readings. Auditors assess groundedness and coherence, not correspondence to a single truth. This is why confirmability is framed as findings being data-grounded rather than objectively verified, and why audits complement rather than replace other quality strategies.

title: What is the debate over preregistration of qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Audit trails & transparency
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is the debate over preregistration of qualitative research?
Answer: Advocates suggest that registering research questions, designs, and analysis plans could increase transparency and distinguish planned from emergent elements. Critics respond that qualitative designs are intentionally iterative and emergent, with questions and sampling evolving through engagement with the field, so preregistration modeled on hypothesis-testing research fits poorly and could pressure researchers into rigidity. Proposed adaptations treat registration as a transparent, updatable record of evolving decisions rather than a binding commitment to fixed hypotheses.

title: What is informed consent?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is informed consent?
Answer: Informed consent is the process by which prospective participants learn what the research involves, including its purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, and their rights, and then freely agree to take part. Valid consent requires adequate information, comprehension, and voluntariness, without coercion or undue influence. In qualitative research it is documented through signed forms, recorded verbal consent, or other approved means, and is best treated as an ongoing process rather than a one-time signature.

title: What is the difference between confidentiality and anonymity?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between confidentiality and anonymity?
Answer: Anonymity means the researcher never collects or cannot link identifying information to responses, so even the researcher does not know who said what. Confidentiality means the researcher knows participants' identities but protects them, withholding identifying details from reports and securing the data. In most qualitative interview research true anonymity is impossible because the researcher meets participants, so the operative promise is confidentiality.

title: Why do researchers use pseudonyms for participants and places?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why do researchers use pseudonyms for participants and places?
Answer: Pseudonyms replace real names of people, organizations, and sometimes locations in transcripts and reports to protect identities while preserving the readability and narrative coherence of the account. They are a standard confidentiality device in qualitative reporting. Researchers should also alter or generalize other identifying details, since a pseudonym alone may not prevent recognition when contextual clues remain.

title: What does the right to withdraw mean?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does the right to withdraw mean?
Answer: Participants may stop taking part at any point without giving a reason and without penalty or loss of benefits to which they are otherwise entitled. Consent materials should explain how to withdraw and what happens to already-collected data, for example whether it will be deleted on request and any practical limits, such as data already anonymized or published. Honoring withdrawal preserves the voluntariness on which ethical research depends.

title: What information should a consent form for a qualitative study include?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What information should a consent form for a qualitative study include?
Answer: It should explain the study's purpose, what participation involves, such as interview length and audio recording, foreseeable risks and benefits, how confidentiality will be protected, how data will be stored and used, including quotations in publications, the voluntary nature of participation and the right to withdraw, and contact details for the researcher and the ethics committee. It should be written in plain language appropriate to the audience. For qualitative work, explicit mention of recording and of how quotes will be used is especially important.

title: What does voluntary participation mean in research ethics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does voluntary participation mean in research ethics?
Answer: Voluntary participation means people join a study by their own free choice, without coercion, pressure from authority figures, or inducements so large they override judgment. It also means participation decisions must not affect unrelated entitlements, such as a patient's care or an employee's standing. Researchers must be especially careful when recruiting through hierarchies, for example when a manager or teacher passes on the invitation.

title: What is debriefing in research ethics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is debriefing in research ethics?
Answer: Debriefing is a conversation or written communication after participation in which the researcher explains the study more fully, answers questions, addresses any discomfort, and, where deception was used, discloses and justifies it. In qualitative research debriefing may also include information about support services when sensitive topics were discussed. It closes the interaction respectfully and gives participants a chance to raise concerns.

title: What does the principle of doing no harm mean in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does the principle of doing no harm mean in qualitative research?
Answer: The principle of nonmaleficence obliges researchers to avoid and minimize harm to participants, which in qualitative research is usually psychological, social, or reputational rather than physical: distress from recalling painful experiences, breach of privacy, or damage from being identifiable in reports. Researchers address it through sensitive interviewing, robust confidentiality protections, careful representation, and support referrals. Harm must be weighed against the study's anticipated benefits, and risks minimized by design.

title: What is process consent?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is process consent?
Answer: Process consent treats consent as ongoing negotiation rather than a single event: the researcher revisits willingness to participate at multiple points, such as at each fieldwork visit, before sensitive interview sections, or as the study's direction evolves. It suits qualitative designs because emergent methods can change what participation involves, and long-term fieldwork relationships can blur the original agreement. It is especially recommended in ethnography and in research with people whose capacity or circumstances fluctuate.

title: Is deception ever acceptable in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Is deception ever acceptable in qualitative research?
Answer: Most ethics frameworks permit deception only when the research question cannot be answered otherwise, the study has significant value, risks are minimal, and participants are debriefed afterward. In qualitative research the main form is covert observation or incomplete disclosure of the study's focus, which conflicts with informed consent and requires strong justification to an ethics committee. The default expectation is openness, with deception as a tightly constrained exception.

title: What are the ethical issues in covert observation?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the ethical issues in covert observation?
Answer: Covert observation denies those observed the opportunity to consent, intrudes on privacy, and risks harm if identities become discernible, so it faces a strong ethical presumption against it. Defenders argue it is sometimes the only way to study concealed or powerful settings, such as closed institutions or deviant groups, and that public behavior carries reduced privacy expectations. Ethics committees typically require evidence that overt methods are impossible, that the knowledge sought is important, and that confidentiality protections are exceptional.

title: What is deductive disclosure and why is it a particular risk in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is deductive disclosure and why is it a particular risk in qualitative research?
Answer: Deductive disclosure occurs when a participant can be identified from the combination of details in a report, such as role, workplace, and distinctive events, even though no name is given. Qualitative reports rely on rich contextual description and verbatim quotes, which makes this risk higher than in aggregated quantitative reporting, and members of the studied community are often the most able to recognize each other. Mitigations include altering or generalizing identifying details, checking quotes for distinctiveness, and considering how findings will read to insiders.

title: What ethical questions arise when using social media posts as qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What ethical questions arise when using social media posts as qualitative data?
Answer: Key questions include whether posts are truly public or shared with an expected limited audience, whether users can meaningfully consent to research use, and whether quoting verbatim enables identification, since exact text is often searchable back to the account. Platform terms, the sensitivity of the topic, and community norms all bear on the analysis. Common safeguards include paraphrasing instead of direct quotation, avoiding usernames, seeking consent for identifiable use, and following guidance such as that of the Association of Internet Researchers.

title: How can participant incentives become ethically problematic?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How can participant incentives become ethically problematic?
Answer: Incentives are acceptable compensation for time and expenses, but they become undue inducement when they are large enough to distort judgment about risks, particularly for economically vulnerable people who may feel unable to refuse. They can also encourage misrepresentation of eligibility. Ethics committees weigh the amount against the population and study burden, and good practice is to compensate fairly for time rather than to pay for risk-taking, and to ensure payment does not depend on completing the study.

title: What are the limits of confidentiality that researchers must disclose to participants?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the limits of confidentiality that researchers must disclose to participants?
Answer: Confidentiality is not absolute: researchers may be legally or professionally obligated to disclose information such as imminent risk of serious harm to the participant or others, or child abuse in jurisdictions with mandatory reporting. Data can also be subject to legal demands in rare cases. Ethical practice requires stating these limits in the consent process so participants can decide what to share, rather than promising unconditional secrecy that cannot be kept.

title: Why is protecting anonymity especially difficult in small communities or organizations?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Why is protecting anonymity especially difficult in small communities or organizations?
Answer: In small settings, members know each other's roles, histories, and manners of speaking, so even heavily de-identified accounts can be recognized from contextual clues like job title, tenure, or a described incident. The risk is internal as much as external: colleagues, family, or neighbors are the likeliest identifiers. Researchers respond by aggregating details, altering non-essential characteristics, omitting some data, negotiating with participants about what can be reported, and sometimes disguising the site itself, while acknowledging these steps trade off descriptive richness.

title: What are ethically important moments in qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What are ethically important moments in qualitative research?
Answer: Guillemin and Gillam distinguished procedural ethics, the approval obtained from committees, from ethics in practice: the unpredictable, ethically important moments that arise in fieldwork, such as a participant disclosing something harmful, becoming distressed, or revealing information about a third party. These moments demand immediate situated judgment that no protocol can fully anticipate. The authors argue that reflexivity is the researcher's chief resource for recognizing and responding well to such moments, making ethics a continuous practice rather than a bureaucratic hurdle.

title: What is relational ethics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is relational ethics?
Answer: Relational ethics grounds ethical conduct in the quality of the relationships between researcher and participants, emphasizing mutual respect, care, dignity, and connectedness rather than rule-following alone. It is prominent in feminist methodology, ethnography, and autoethnography, where long-term relationships and intimate knowledge create obligations that outlast data collection, including care in how people are represented. From this perspective, questions like how one writes about a friend-informant are ethical questions as weighty as consent procedures.

title: What ethical issues surround the representation of participants in published findings?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What ethical issues surround the representation of participants in published findings?
Answer: Representation raises questions beyond confidentiality: whether the account portrays participants fairly or reduces them to stereotypes, whose voice frames the narrative, and how participants will feel and fare when they read unflattering but evidenced interpretations. Critical findings about a community can cause collective harm even when individuals are unidentifiable. Researchers navigate this through reflexive attention to voice, sharing findings with participants, contextualizing negative portrayals, and weighing scholarly candor against the risk of harm to those depicted.

title: How should consent be handled in ethnographic research in public or semi-public settings?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Ethics fundamentals
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: How should consent be handled in ethnographic research in public or semi-public settings?
Answer: Ethnographers often cannot obtain individual consent from everyone present in a public plaza, hospital corridor, or online forum, so ethics frameworks allow observation of public behavior with reduced consent requirements, provided individuals are not identified and privacy expectations are respected. Good practice includes obtaining consent from key informants and gatekeepers, announcing the researcher's presence where feasible, and applying heightened protections in semi-public spaces where people expect limited audiences. The guiding questions are what privacy those present reasonably expect and what risks identification would create.

title: What is an Institutional Review Board?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is an Institutional Review Board?
Answer: An Institutional Review Board, or IRB, is a committee, in the United States and institutions following its model, that reviews proposed research with human participants before it begins, to ensure risks are minimized and reasonable relative to benefits, consent is adequate, and participant rights and welfare are protected. IRBs can approve studies, require modifications, or disapprove them, and they conduct continuing oversight. Equivalent bodies elsewhere are commonly called research ethics committees.

title: What is a research ethics committee?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is a research ethics committee?
Answer: A research ethics committee, or REC, is the general term, used in the United Kingdom, Europe, and many other regions, for the body that reviews human research proposals for ethical acceptability, paralleling the American IRB. It examines the study's risks and benefits, consent procedures, confidentiality protections, and recruitment fairness. Approval from such a committee is typically required before data collection and is expected by journals and funders.

title: What is meant by a vulnerable population in research ethics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is meant by a vulnerable population in research ethics?
Answer: Vulnerable populations are groups with diminished capacity or freedom to protect their own interests in research, whether through limited decision-making capacity, dependent relationships, or social and economic disadvantage. Commonly cited examples include children, prisoners, people with cognitive impairments, and economically or educationally disadvantaged persons. Research with such groups requires additional safeguards, such as modified consent processes, advocates, or stricter risk limits.

title: What is the difference between consent and assent when researching children?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is the difference between consent and assent when researching children?
Answer: Because minors generally lack legal capacity to consent, a parent or guardian provides informed permission for the child's participation, while the child provides assent, an affirmative, age-appropriate agreement to take part. Assent requires explaining the study in terms the child can understand and respecting refusal even when the guardian has agreed. Both are typically required, with the form of assent adapted to the child's developmental stage.

title: What does minimal risk mean in ethics review?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does minimal risk mean in ethics review?
Answer: Minimal risk means the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during routine physical or psychological examinations. It is a threshold used to determine review level and permissible research designs, especially with vulnerable groups. Many qualitative interview studies are judged minimal risk, though sensitive topics can raise the assessment.

title: What is expedited review?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is expedited review?
Answer: Expedited review is a streamlined procedure in which one or a few designated reviewers, rather than the full convened board, evaluate research that poses no more than minimal risk and falls within specified categories, which often include interviews, focus groups, and surveys. It applies the same ethical criteria as full review but proceeds faster. Studies involving greater risk or certain vulnerable populations generally still require full board review.

title: Why do qualitative studies need ethics review if they seem low risk?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why do qualitative studies need ethics review if they seem low risk?
Answer: Qualitative research can still cause real harm: distress from probing sensitive experiences, breach of confidentiality, identification through rich description, and exploitation of dependent relationships. Ethics review provides independent scrutiny of consent, confidentiality, and recruitment before these risks materialize. Review also protects researchers and institutions and is a precondition for publication in most fields.

title: What materials are typically submitted for ethics review of a qualitative study?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What materials are typically submitted for ethics review of a qualitative study?
Answer: A typical submission includes the protocol describing aims, design, sampling, and procedures; recruitment materials; participant information sheets and consent forms; interview guides or topic guides; and a data management plan covering storage, access, confidentiality, and retention. Committees may also ask about researcher training, distress protocols, and plans for reporting quotes. Because qualitative designs evolve, submissions often explain how emergent changes will be handled through amendments.

title: What are the Belmont Report principles and how do they apply to qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What are the Belmont Report principles and how do they apply to qualitative research?
Answer: The Belmont Report articulates three principles: respect for persons, requiring informed consent and protection of those with diminished autonomy; beneficence, requiring harms to be minimized and benefits maximized; and justice, requiring fair distribution of research burdens and benefits. In qualitative research these translate into ongoing consent practices, careful handling of sensitive disclosures and confidentiality, and equitable, non-exploitative selection of participants and communities. The report underpins the United States regulatory framework and remains a touchstone for research ethics generally.

title: What role do gatekeepers play in research access, and what ethical issues do they raise?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What role do gatekeepers play in research access, and what ethical issues do they raise?
Answer: Gatekeepers are people who control access to a setting or population, such as school heads, clinic managers, or community leaders, and researchers usually need their permission to recruit. Ethically, gatekeeper approval must not substitute for individual consent, and gatekeeper involvement can compromise voluntariness if members feel monitored or pressured, or can bias sampling if the gatekeeper filters who is invited. Researchers should recruit in ways that keep individual participation decisions private from the gatekeeper wherever possible.

title: How should researchers assess capacity to consent in adults with cognitive impairment?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should researchers assess capacity to consent in adults with cognitive impairment?
Answer: Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate, so researchers assess whether the person can understand the study information, retain it, weigh it in reaching a decision, and communicate a choice, using simplified materials and repeated explanation where helpful. Impairment does not automatically preclude participation; excluding people unnecessarily is itself an injustice that silences their perspectives. Where capacity is lacking, frameworks typically allow proxy consent from a legal representative combined with the person's assent and respect for signs of dissent.

title: Why do prisoners receive special protections in research ethics?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: Why do prisoners receive special protections in research ethics?
Answer: Incarceration constrains voluntariness: prisoners may perceive participation as linked to privileges, parole prospects, or staff approval, and the institutional environment limits genuinely free refusal. Historical abuses of prisoners in research also motivated explicit safeguards, such as the additional protections in United States regulations restricting permissible categories of prison research. Reviews of prison studies scrutinize recruitment, incentives, confidentiality from institutional staff, and whether the research addresses questions relevant to prisoners themselves.

title: What ethical issues arise when researchers study their own students or employees?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What ethical issues arise when researchers study their own students or employees?
Answer: The power the researcher holds over grades, references, or employment can compromise voluntariness, since refusal may feel risky and consent may be given to please. There are also confidentiality hazards, because the researcher will continue to interact with participants and knows their identities intimately. Safeguards include recruitment and consent handled by a third party, anonymized participation where feasible, explicit assurance that participation has no bearing on assessment or employment, and sometimes choosing a different population altogether.

title: How should emergent design changes in qualitative research be handled with an ethics committee?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should emergent design changes in qualitative research be handled with an ethics committee?
Answer: Substantive changes, such as new participant groups, revised interview topics, added data types, or altered consent procedures, should be submitted as amendments and approved before implementation. Researchers can reduce friction by writing protocols that anticipate emergence, describing the range of likely adaptations and the decision principles that will govern them. Minor wording changes to guides usually fall within an approved protocol, but anything affecting risk, consent, or confidentiality requires review.

title: What distress protocol should qualitative researchers prepare for sensitive interviews?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What distress protocol should qualitative researchers prepare for sensitive interviews?
Answer: A distress protocol specifies how the interviewer will respond if a participant becomes upset: pausing or stopping the interview, offering breaks, reminding the participant of the right to withdraw, and providing pre-identified support resources such as counseling services or helplines. It may define escalation steps for disclosures of risk of harm and specify follow-up contact. Ethics committees commonly require such protocols for studies on trauma, illness, bereavement, and similar topics, and interviewers should be trained in applying them.

title: How do ethics committees evaluate compensation for vulnerable participants?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How do ethics committees evaluate compensation for vulnerable participants?
Answer: Committees ask whether the amount fairly compensates time and expenses without becoming an undue inducement that overrides risk judgment, a concern heightened where participants are economically deprived or dependent. They also consider the payment form, since cash, vouchers, or services carry different implications in different settings, and whether payment is contingent on completing the study, which can undermine the right to withdraw. The prevailing standard is fair, non-contingent compensation proportionate to burden.

title: What criticisms have qualitative researchers made of IRB review?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What criticisms have qualitative researchers made of IRB review?
Answer: A long-standing critique is that review systems were built around biomedical, hypothesis-testing research and fit poorly with emergent qualitative designs, demanding fixed instruments, specified sample sizes, and one-off consent that qualitative fieldwork cannot honestly promise. Critics also point to inconsistent decisions across committees and to reviewers unfamiliar with qualitative epistemologies who misjudge its risks. Responses include qualitative-specific guidance for committees, qualitative expertise on boards, and proportionate review pathways for minimal-risk social research.

title: What is ethics creep?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What is ethics creep?
Answer: Ethics creep describes the expansion of ethics regulation in intensity and scope, with review bodies governing ever more activities and demanding ever more procedural compliance, a trend analyzed critically by scholars such as Kevin Haggerty. Critics argue it burdens low-risk social research, encourages box-ticking over genuine ethical reflection, and can push researchers away from studying sensitive or powerful subjects. Defenders counter that expanded oversight responds to real historical harms; the debate concerns proportionality, not whether review should exist.

title: Why do some scholars argue vulnerability should be understood contextually rather than categorically?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Why do some scholars argue vulnerability should be understood contextually rather than categorically?
Answer: Categorical approaches label whole groups, such as prisoners or people with disabilities, as vulnerable, which can be paternalistic, stigmatizing, and exclusionary, denying those groups a voice in research about their lives. Contextual approaches instead ask what specific features of a situation, such as dependency on the researcher, precarious status, or topic sensitivity, create vulnerability for particular people in a particular study. This view directs safeguards at actual sources of risk and recognizes that anyone can be vulnerable in some research circumstances while nominally vulnerable groups can participate safely with appropriate design.

title: What are the ethical arguments for and against excluding vulnerable groups from research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: IRB & vulnerable populations
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: What are the ethical arguments for and against excluding vulnerable groups from research?
Answer: Exclusion protects people with limited capacity or freedom from exploitation and harm, honoring beneficence and respect for persons. But blanket exclusion violates justice: it deprives those groups of evidence about their own conditions, silences their perspectives, and shifts research benefits to less burdened populations. Contemporary ethics therefore favors inclusion with safeguards, adapted consent, advocates, heightened confidentiality, and risk limits, over exclusion, reserving exclusion for cases where risks genuinely cannot be managed.

title: What are the basics of secure storage for qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What are the basics of secure storage for qualitative data?
Answer: Digital data should be stored on encrypted, password-protected, institutionally approved systems with access limited to the research team, and physical materials such as consent forms and notes kept in locked storage. Identifiable data should be separated from de-identified data, and backups maintained securely. Personal laptops, unencrypted portable drives, and unapproved consumer cloud accounts are common points of failure to avoid.

title: What is anonymization of qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is anonymization of qualitative data?
Answer: Anonymization is the process of removing or altering information so that individuals can no longer be identified, directly or indirectly, from the data. In qualitative material this goes beyond deleting names to handling indirect identifiers such as job titles, places, dates, and distinctive events. Fully irreversible anonymization is difficult for rich qualitative data, which is why many projects more accurately describe their data as de-identified or pseudonymized.

title: What is de-identification?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What is de-identification?
Answer: De-identification is the removal or masking of direct identifiers, such as names, addresses, and contact details, and the reduction of indirect identifiers that could reveal who a participant is. It is often performed during or immediately after transcription, with pseudonyms or codes replacing names. De-identification reduces re-identification risk but does not necessarily eliminate it, especially when rich contextual detail remains.

title: Why is a linkage key kept separate from research data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Why is a linkage key kept separate from research data?
Answer: A linkage key is the file that connects participant codes or pseudonyms to real identities, needed for tasks such as follow-up contact or withdrawal requests. Storing it separately from the data, in a differently secured location with tighter access, means that a breach of the dataset alone does not expose identities. Destroying the key when it is no longer needed converts pseudonymized data into effectively anonymized data.

title: How should audio and video recordings be handled securely?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How should audio and video recordings be handled securely?
Answer: Recordings are among the most identifying materials a study holds, since voices and faces cannot be pseudonymized in place, so they should be transferred promptly from recording devices to encrypted storage and deleted from the devices. Access should be limited to those who need it for transcription and analysis, and consent should state how long recordings are kept. Many protocols destroy recordings after transcription is verified, retaining only de-identified transcripts.

title: How long should qualitative research data be retained?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: How long should qualitative research data be retained?
Answer: Retention follows the period stated in the ethics protocol and consent forms, shaped by institutional, funder, and legal requirements; common norms range from five to ten years after study completion to support verification and any queries about the work. Identifiable materials are usually destroyed sooner than de-identified data, and recordings often earliest of all. When the retention period ends, data should be destroyed securely, not simply deleted.

title: Who should have access to identifiable qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: Who should have access to identifiable qualitative data?
Answer: Access should follow the need-to-know principle: only named members of the research team whose roles require it, as specified in the ethics protocol and consent materials, such as the interviewer and transcriber. Supervisors, auditors, or translators may be granted defined access under confidentiality obligations. Access lists should be documented, and sharing identifiable data with anyone outside the approved circle requires new consent or ethics approval.

title: What does secure data destruction involve?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Beginner
Question: What does secure data destruction involve?
Answer: Secure destruction means rendering data unrecoverable: shredding or incinerating paper records and using secure deletion methods, degaussing, or physical destruction for digital media, since ordinary deletion leaves recoverable traces. It applies to all copies, including backups, portable devices, and recordings, and should occur at the time promised in the consent and protocol. Documenting destruction, what, when, and how, completes the data lifecycle in the audit trail.

title: What is the difference between pseudonymization and anonymization under the GDPR?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is the difference between pseudonymization and anonymization under the GDPR?
Answer: Under the European General Data Protection Regulation, pseudonymized data, where identifiers are replaced but a key or other means could re-link individuals, remain personal data and stay within the regulation's scope, requiring a lawful basis, security measures, and respect for data subject rights. Anonymized data, where identification is no longer reasonably possible by any party, fall outside the regulation entirely. Because rich qualitative data are rarely truly anonymous, most qualitative datasets in Europe should be treated as pseudonymized personal data with full protections.

title: What should researchers consider before using cloud services for qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What should researchers consider before using cloud services for qualitative data?
Answer: Key considerations are whether the service is approved by the institution and covered by an appropriate data processing agreement, where the servers are located, since cross-border storage can trigger legal transfer requirements, and whether encryption protects data in transit and at rest. Consumer-grade accounts on personal terms are generally unsuitable for identifiable data. Access controls, audit logging, and the provider's rights over stored content should also be checked against the promises made to participants.

title: What precautions apply when outsourcing transcription to third parties?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What precautions apply when outsourcing transcription to third parties?
Answer: External transcribers hear fully identifiable recordings, so they must be bound by written confidentiality or data processing agreements, receive files through secure transfer rather than email, and delete all copies after delivery. The arrangement should be disclosed in the ethics protocol and, ideally, in consent materials. Automated transcription services raise parallel questions about where audio is processed, whether it is retained or used to train systems, and whether the provider's terms are compatible with confidentiality promises.

title: What is data minimization and how does it apply to qualitative research?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What is data minimization and how does it apply to qualitative research?
Answer: Data minimization is the principle, codified in the GDPR, that only personal data necessary for the research purpose should be collected and retained. In qualitative practice this means not gathering identifying or sensitive details without analytic need, de-identifying at the earliest feasible stage, destroying recordings once verified transcripts exist if recordings are not needed, and limiting demographic collection to what the analysis requires. Minimization reduces both breach impact and participant risk without compromising depth on the phenomena that matter.

title: What issues arise when qualitative data cross national borders?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What issues arise when qualitative data cross national borders?
Answer: International collaborations and cloud services can move personal data between jurisdictions with different legal protections, which regulations such as the GDPR restrict unless safeguards like adequacy decisions or standard contractual clauses are in place. Researchers must know where their storage and transcription providers actually process data and whether collaborators abroad may lawfully receive identifiable material. Practical solutions include sharing only de-identified data across borders, using institutionally approved platforms, and specifying transfer arrangements in the ethics protocol and consent documents.

title: How should field notes be protected when they contain identifiable observations?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: How should field notes be protected when they contain identifiable observations?
Answer: Field notes often record names, roles, and recognizable events before any de-identification, so notebooks should be kept physically secure during fieldwork, avoid full names where memory aids suffice, and be transcribed into encrypted digital form promptly with identifiers coded. Researchers in sensitive settings sometimes maintain a separate key for people and places. Because notes may also capture information about non-consented third parties, extra care applies to what is written down at all.

title: What data protection questions should researchers ask before using AI tools on interview data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What data protection questions should researchers ask before using AI tools on interview data?
Answer: Before submitting transcripts or audio to AI transcription or analysis services, researchers should establish where the data are processed, whether the provider stores them or uses them for model training, whether an institutional agreement governs the processing, and whether participants' consent covers this use. Identifiable data should not enter tools that lack contractual confidentiality guarantees, and de-identification before upload reduces risk. Ethics committees and data protection officers increasingly expect these questions to be answered in the protocol.

title: What should a data management plan for a qualitative study cover?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Intermediate
Question: What should a data management plan for a qualitative study cover?
Answer: A data management plan specifies what data will be collected and in what forms, where and how each type will be stored and secured, who will have access and under what conditions, how and when de-identification will occur, retention and destruction schedules, and any plans for sharing or archiving. It should align with the consent materials so participants are promised only what the plan can deliver. Funders and ethics committees increasingly require such plans at the proposal stage.

title: Why is re-identification risk especially high for rich qualitative data?
content:
Domain: Qualitative research methodology
Category: Quality, Rigor & Ethics
Subcategory: Data protection & secure handling
Difficulty: Advanced
Question: Why is re-identification risk especially high for rich qualitative data?
Answer: Qualitative value lies in contextual specificity, detailed narratives, unusual events, precise roles and relationships, and this same specificity functions as a quasi-identifier: the combination of a few details can single out one person even with names removed.
